value.text: President Donald Trump and FBI Director Kash Patel are paying tribute to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office detective killed in a Thanksgiving morning wrong-way crash on Interstate 95.Speaking in Palm Beach on Thursday, Trump offered his condolences to the fallen detective's family."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, an expert at bombs and explosives, who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty," Trump said.Authorities have since identified the fallen detective as Alan Smith, 46, of West Palm Beach.Trump did not identify Smith during his remarks Thursday, citing ongoing efforts to notify his family and others.In a statement posted on X, Patel revealed Smith had served nearly 20 years with the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office and had extensive experience investigating explosives-related crimes.Smith graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013 and served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, according to Patel."This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe," Patel wrote. "Never forget them and their families."Smith leaves behind a wife and 14-year-old son.The Florida Highway Patrol said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol vehicle south on I-95 just north of Military Trail shortly after 5 a.m. Thursday, when a driver traveling in the wrong direction collided with him head-on.Smith was on duty and headed to work at the time of the crash, according to the sheriff's office. He was airlifted to St. Mary's Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead.Troopers identified the wrong-way driver as Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, of Palm Beach Gardens.Investigators said Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash and was driving despite three prior DUI convictions and an active 10-year driver's license revocation.Trump also addressed the circumstances surrounding the deadly collision."It was a drunk driver — really drunk driver," Trump said. "He was going on the opposite side of the highway, if you can believe it. And so it's a terrible thing that happened."Espinoza Martinez was hospitalized with serious injuries and arrested Thursday afternoon.Members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office joined troopers at the hospital, placing Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective, according to FHP.Troopers said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail upon his release from the hospital on multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide and aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer.The Florida Highway Patrol continues to investigate the crash.

Alan’s legacy of service, knowledge, compassion, and dedication to others will never be forgotten.— PBSO (@PBCountySheriff) November 26, 2026 The sheriff's office said Smith was driving an unmarked patrol car at the time of the crash. Espinoza Martinez was also taken to St. Mary's Medical Center with incapacitating injuries.All lanes were back open at about noon after the closure lasted about seven hours.The Florida Highway Patrol said at about 2:33 p.m., troopers arrested Espinoza Martinez in connection with the fatal wrong-way crash. The arrest took place at St. Mary's Medical Center, according to FHP."Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Espinoza Martinez in the handcuffs carried by the fallen detective," FHP said in a statement.According to FHP, Espinoza Martinez was intoxicated at the time of the crash, with an active license revocation for 10 years and three prior DUI convictions.Upon his release from the hospital, FHP said Espinoza Martinez will be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail on the following charges:Vehicular HomicideDUI ManslaughterAggravated BatteryAggravated Battery on a Law Enforcement OfficerDriving While License Suspended or Revoked Causing Death or Serious Bodily InjuryDriving While License Suspended or Revoked – Subsequent OffenseDUI Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonReckless Driving Causing Damage to Property or Injury to Another PersonFHP said they are investigating the circumstances of the crash.President Donald Trump made a statement about the crash during a press conference on Thursday, according to CNN."I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, uh, an expert at bombs and explosives who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty and I'm not able to release his name yet. They, they're notifying the family and notifying a lot of people.

While many families gathered around the dinner table Thursday, Bill Caesar spent his Thanksgiving making sure those without a table to gather around weren't forgotten.Inside a Delray Beach home, about 40 volunteers worked together to pack 350 plates of hot food, complete with turkey, mashed potatoes and string beans.It's a Thanksgiving tradition Caesar has carried on for about 15 years through his charity, Coming Back to Give Back.WATCH: More than a meal: Delray Beach man spends Thanksgiving feeding those in need"I got here at 4 o'clock this morning," Caesar said.For thousands of Floridians, Thanksgiving looks vastly different from the holiday many have come to know. More than 24,000 people are experiencing homelessness statewide, including more than 1,500 in Palm Beach County alone. Others face financial hardship, isolation or limited mobility.Caesar wants to make sure those circumstances don't keep anyone from enjoying a Thanksgiving meal."It's a great feeling whenever you can give back," said Caesar. And for those who can't come to him, he goes to them.One of his stops Thursday was Lakes of Delray, a senior living community where he delivered 50 meals to residents, some of whom have difficulty leaving their homes or don't have family nearby."Can’t get around, so we're bringing it to them," Caesar said.From there, Caesar headed to a bus station, where he delivered a Thanksgiving dinner to a woman named Pauline, who has recently fallen on hard times."Special delivery!" Caesar said as he approached her.He handed her a plate of food, checked on her, and wished her a blessed Thanksgiving.Throughout the day, Caesar did more than distribute meals. He introduced himself, struck up conversations and connected with people throughout the community.For Caesar, the food is a way to offer something more: human connection."It's a great day brightening everybody else's day and making sure everyone's good," Caesar said after sitting and talking with a man named Willie. "He was like, ecstatic; he was like, 'Oh my god, I didn't have a meal, I didn't know what I was going to do today." On a holiday centered around togetherness, even a brief conversation can carry meaning for someone accustomed to being overlooked.For people like Willie, Anthony and Jamie, whom Caesar visited Thursday, the greatest gift of Thanksgiving may not be what's on the plate, but the reminder that someone cares.Because sometimes, it's not just about having a place to get a meal.It's about feeling like you have a place in the world.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Two Palm Beach County home-based baking businesses are turning a love of baking into neighborhood side hustles, using social media to connect with customers without opening traditional storefronts.WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache first noticed the small bakery stands appearing on her own TikTok feed. She connected with Sweet Marie’s in West Palm Beach and DynastyDough in Boca Raton to learn how the entrepreneurs behind them are building businesses from home.WATCH: Palm Beach County home bakers build businesses through social mediaA mother-daughter business in West Palm BeachAlong Florida Avenue in West Palm Beach, Nicola Billows and her mother, Celina Billows, operate Sweet Marie’s.The two told WPTV they both have full-time jobs. “So I was like, mom, let’s make this come to life.”Before opening their stand, the pair said they distributed hundreds of free samples throughout their neighborhood. Customers can now stop by their Florida Avenue stand Monday through Saturday.Celina Billows said balancing the bakery with her career can be demanding.“It’s definitely a challenge to balance both my job and then baking, but you know what, we make it work,” she said.For her daughter, the business offers another kind of benefit.“My job can be, like, very heavy and overwhelming most nights, so this is just such a good outlet,” Nicola Billows said.Operating a small neighborhood stand also requires trust. Sweet Marie’s uses an honor system, which Celina Billows said has left her encouraged by the community’s response.“I have had my faith restored in humanity,” she said. “There are so many wonderful people, and we are on an honor system and, like, every day, we’re amazed.”A few miles away, another baker is finding his own community of customers.DynastyDough grows in Boca RatonAlong Northwest 35th Lane in Boca Raton, Peyton Ming operates DynastyDough while also working full-time as a Realtor.Ming told WPTV he has baked since he was young. He built his bakery stand using recycled materials given to him by people in the community.“What better way to connect with the community than to sell bread in the community?” Ming said. “I just think that food and good bread in general brings people together.”DynastyDough offers items including bread, muffins and bagels, with pre-order pickups available on Fridays.Ming said the response after promoting his business on social media caught him by surprise.“I had so many people come by on the very first week, and I was shocked,” he said.Florida cottage food law allows home-based businesses to operateHome-based food businesses such as these operate under rules established by Florida law.Under Florida’s cottage food law, a qualifying cottage food operation is exempt from the state's food permitting requirement if it follows the law and does not exceed $250,000 in annual gross sales of cottage food products. The law also allows cottage food businesses to sell and accept payments online, but prohibits wholesale sales. Florida law includes additional requirements governing eligible cottage food operations and product labeling.For entrepreneurs such as Ming, running a business from home allows work and community to intersect.“Of course, it’s still a job, but it feels much more real life when I’m able to connect with the community and do it from the comfort of my own home and my own neighborhood,” he said.Neither business owner knows exactly where the venture will take them. For now, they are continuing to bake, post on social media and build their customer bases one order at a time.Asked what he would tell someone who has an idea but is hesitant to pursue it, Ming offered advice from his own experience.“You can do something and start something scared and learn along the way,” he said. “That’s something that I really fall back on every time, and I think about how far I’ve come.”Where to find themSweet Marie’s is located at 1211 Florida Ave., West Palm Beach, FL 33401. For updates on availability and bakery stand information, follow Sweet Marie’s on Instagram. For DynastyDough pickup and location information, visit DynastyDough on TikTok. Black Friday shoppers were out early across South Florida on Friday, with some music fans waiting for hours to get their hands on limited-edition vinyl releases.About 80 people lined up outside Rust & Wax record store in West Palm Beach as shoppers sought special limited-edition Record Store Day releases from artists including The Beatles, Cher, Sombr, the Grateful Dead and Stevie Nicks.WATCH REPORT BELOW:T.A. Walker caught up with Diane of Palm Beach Gardens, a Stevie Nicks fan who arrived around midnight and scored one of the records on her wish list. She was among the first customers inside the store Friday morning and had her sights set on a special Stevie Nicks release of "Bella Donna.""She took the face of the 'Bella Donna' album and imprinted it directly on the actual album itself," Diane told Walker. "So when you're listening to 'Bella Donna,' you're actually seeing Stevie Nicks."The early-morning rush wasn't limited to record collectors.Shoppers were also heading to retailers and shopping centers across the area, including Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Macy's, Kohl's, The Mall at Wellington Green, The Gardens Mall, Town Center at Boca Raton and Treasure Coast Square.The crowds come as many consumers still plan to do at least some of their holiday shopping in person.According to holiday shopping research cited by Accenture, 66% of consumers plan to hunt for Black Friday or Cyber Monday deals at brick-and-mortar stores rather than doing all of their shopping online.The research also found the average consumer is expected to spend about $737 this holiday season.For the music fans waiting outside Rust & Wax, however, Black Friday was about more than simply finding a discount. It was a chance to be among the first to grab a limited-edition release before it disappeared from the shelves.What do you want me to Shine A Light on? What are you most proud of where you live? Email me at tawalker@wptv.com.

Thanksgiving travelers at President Donald J. Trump International Airport were navigating dozens of delayed flights Wednesday, but WPTV observed no cancellations during its reporting as millions of Americans took to the skies ahead of the holiday.WATCH BELOW: Thanksgiving travelers navigate delaysThe Transportation Security Administration (TSA) expects to screen about 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Tuesday and Monday, with more than 3 million passengers expected Sunday, the busiest day of the Thanksgiving travel period.Nationwide, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is forecasting more than 417,000 flights during the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period. The federal agency has also warned that weather could affect flights as storms move across several parts of the country. Across South Florida, conditions varied Wednesday. Travelers reported long security lines at Miami International Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport, while FlightAware recorded more than 1,100 delays nationwide Wednesday morning.Despite delays, many travelers WPTV met in Palm Beach County were focused less on the wait and more on who was waiting for them at the end of the trip.Yvonne Jackson arrived from Toronto to spend Thanksgiving with family."The end result is we're here, we're happy, and we can't wait to be with the family tomorrow," Jackson said.Her flight took longer than expected as weather complicated the final approach."The pilot said they had to circle because the ground was too wet, so we were up there in the clouds and just felt a bit nervous," Jackson said.Eventually, the flight made it to the ground."Finally, he landed with a thud, and we all clapped," she said.On the other side of the arrival doors, Debbie Hunter was waiting for a reunion of her own."I'm here to pick up my son," Hunter said. "He's flying in from Washington, D.C. for Thanksgiving."Her son recently turned 32, making the homecoming a celebration of both his birthday and the holiday."Extremely excited," Hunter said. "I love to have my young man come home."While some families were welcoming relatives home, Barbara Cook and Brian Cook were preparing to fly out to see theirs."We were expecting the worst," they said. "So far, it hasn't been too bad."Their flight to New York's LaGuardia Airport was delayed, meaning their reunion with their daughter and her family would have to wait."Probably won't see our family till tomorrow," they said.But there is an especially important reason to make the trip."She has a newborn and a 2-year-old," Barbara Cook said. "So we're excited to see our 10th grandchild."Brian Cook summed up the motivation behind the holiday journey."It's all about family," he said.The TSA recommends arriving at least two hours before a domestic flight and three hours before an international flight during the busy Thanksgiving travel period.TSA says passengers should also allow extra time for parking, airline check-in, checking bags and security screening. Travelers should check directly with their airline for the latest flight information before leaving for the airport. The FAA is also encouraging passengers to plan ahead because weather could affect flights throughout the holiday week. For many travelers making their way through Palm Beach County on Wednesday, however, the delays were easier to accept knowing family was waiting at the other end.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Another round of heavy rain in Florida is once again raising concerns about flooding and flood insurance. According to the Insurance Information Institute, as much as 80% of Florida homeowners don't carry flood insurance, even though just one inch of water in a home can cause $25,000 in damage.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "Everyone is in a flood zone," says Lee Wiglesworth of Wiglesworth Rindom Insurance in Stuart. "It's just a matter of if you're in a high risk or a low risk." He said many pass on the coverage because of costs, being in a low-risk zone and also not fully understanding their homeowners policy. "If a hurricane comes and creates a flooding event, they think I have hurricane coverage," he said. But those claims are often denied since homeowners policies only cover wind damage. Experts say relying on FEMA in flood situations can leave homeowners short, since FEMA grants will cover temporary housing and essential repairs. National flood insurance will cover $250,000 on the structure and $100,000 on the contents of a home. Costs for flood insurance can vary from $600 to $1,300 a year. In addition to national flood insurance, there are also options for flood insurance with private insurers, and there are waiting periods before policies become active.

Heavy rain moved across the area Wednesday, flooding roads in parts of West Palm Beach. The soggy weather created a messy drive as people prepared to travel for Thanksgiving.Several areas of downtown West Palm Beach saw significant standing water as rain continued to fall.WATCH REPORT BELOW: At South Flagler Drive and Barcelona Road, water covered the roadway, forcing some drivers to turn around rather than attempt to make it through.WPTV reporter Christy Waite saw several cars turn around to avoid the area.Flooding was visible across several parts of the city. Near Ann Norton Sculpture Gardens, Palm Beach Atlantic University and the Palm Beach County Yacht Club, streets filled with water and even traffic cones could be seen floating in the roadway.Across from Elisabetta's Ristorante in downtown West Palm Beach, the water rose past Waite's boot as vehicles, including buses, continued navigating the flooded streets.From downtown, Waite traveled north to Lone Pine Estates in Riviera Beach, a neighborhood that has been hit especially hard by flooding this month.Neighbor Lacey Stone previously described how quickly conditions deteriorated."I have lived in Florida my whole life, and I have never seen anything like this; it just got worse and worse," Stone said.The water in the neighborhood has since receded, but signs of the earlier flooding remain.Some residents still have sandbags outside their homes, while others continue dealing with damage left behind. Residents like Stephanie Gabriel never want to experience something like this again. "This has been a devastating experience, and seeing all the damage it has caused is heart-wrenching," Gabriel said.The flooding wasn't limited to the areas WPTV visited.As Waite headed back to the station, she found even more standing water, this time in WPTV’s own parking lot in West Palm Beach.

Federal disaster aid is now available for residents in Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast affected by recent flooding.FEMA announced late Tuesday that federal disaster assistance is available to individuals and families in Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Brevard counties as recovery efforts continue.U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said in a statement the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments devastated by the flooding.The assistance can include grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster.Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider. They can then apply for FEMA assistance through DisasterAssistance.gov, by calling 1-800-621-3362 or through the FEMA App.Those who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should provide FEMA with the number for that service when applying.Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance is available in Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee, counties.Frankel said that Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide — nearly $35 million to help individuals and families recover and more than $18 million to help local governments cover emergency response and cleanup costs.Additional counties could be designated for federal assistance later, depending on the results of continuing damage assessments.What residents should do:File a claim with their insurance provider.Apply for federal assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362.Severe storms and flooding have impacted parts of Florida since Oct. 31, prompting the state to ask for the federal disaster declaration.

Millions of people are hitting the road this Thanksgiving holiday, but getting to their final destination isn't always going according to plan.Heavy rain moved across South Florida on Wednesday, adding another challenge for drivers traveling to spend the holiday with family and friends.WATCH WPTV'S COVERAGE HERE: Even with rain in the forecast, some travelers weren't prepared for the unexpected delays they encountered along the way.More than 4.2 million Floridians are expected to travel by car for Thanksgiving, according to AAA. Nationwide, the Federal Aviation Administration also expects more than 417,000 flights during the nine-day Thanksgiving travel period, making it the busiest Thanksgiving travel stretch in 16 years.For many travelers, the goal was simply getting home."I haven't been home in like a month and a half," one traveler said.Others were making their way to South Florida, including one man who said, "We're trying to get to Miami."But the journey became more complicated for drivers on Florida's Turnpike in Palm Beach County.A jackknifed tractor-trailer shut down the southbound lanes, leaving drivers stuck in standstill traffic. The delay was an unexpected hurdle for people already navigating wet roads and holiday congestion.One man making the trip from Georgia to Miami was among those caught in the backup. Another traveler said a drive that typically takes two hours had quickly turned into three."We knew it was going to rain today all day long," one driver said.Another woman said she expected some delays because of the weather but was surprised by how long traffic had come to a stop."Well, we didn't expect to be sitting here an hour for sure. We expected some delays because of rain and potential flooding," she said.The delay was so significant that she was considering changing her plans altogether."We actually might, because it's been so long, might turn around and go back to my daughter's house, in West Palm Beach," she said.Others found ways to make the unexpected wait a little more entertaining. One child said the family was passing the time by playing a game."We're playing like a Heads Up game," the child said.For another traveler, the immediate priority was getting traffic moving again — and finding a bathroom."So we're just hoping this gets moving soon so we can find a Jiffy John somewhere," the traveler said.Despite the rain and unexpected traffic backups, travelers shared one common goal: making it to their loved ones in time for Thanksgiving.For drivers still making the trip, officials recommend allowing extra travel time, slowing down on wet roads and staying alert for changing traffic conditions.

A water meter data collection issue in Martin County caused some utility customers to receive unusually high water bills, according to Martin County Utilities.The county said the problem dates back about five months and affected the reporting of water usage for some customers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: After the issue was corrected, water usage that had not previously been reported was reflected on a single month's bill, resulting in a higher-than-normal charge for affected customers.Martin County Utilities said the issue affects some customers in these communities:Legacy CoveHighlands ReserveCove IsleMontego CoveEmerald LakesSavannah OaksCove LakesRiver MarinaRiver Marina EstatesRocky PointCustomers with questions about their bills or who need assistance can contact Martin County Utilities customer service at cservice@martin.fl.us. The county said a customer service representative can work with affected residents to establish a payment arrangement.Martin County Utilities said it has since implemented additional training and safeguards within its data collection software.Have you been affected? Let us know on our Facebook page!

In Fort Pierce, behind the doors of A Future Worth Fighting 4, they embody what the City stands for.“Here, this community is a big fighting community. If you’re from Fort Pierce, you know how we get down," owner Darrion Henry said.How they get down at A Future Worth Fighting 4 was on full display at the 2026 Florida State Police Athletic League.WATCH: A local boxing gym brings the two C's: community and championshipsThey finished with three state champions, a silver medalist, and a second-place overall team finish, and the star of the Tournament was none other than Justice Henry. He credits the gym's family-like atmosphere and tough-love environment for his success.“This gym has been the biggest part of my life. I’ve been boxing since I was eight years old, and this became a home for our own little community and us, with everyone we bring in here,” said Henry.While Henry has been boxing since he was eight, he has a teammate, Frantzner Jean, who’s just getting started but is already making a name for himself after winning his first fight by unanimous decision.“It felt pretty fun; I just like the dopamine rush from it,” said Jean.Every day after school, kids fill the gym to learn the sweet science of boxing, but there's one rule: you have to go to school every day.“I’m a teacher at Dan McCarty, so I can see how their behavior has changed, and now I have a lot of kids who show up to school because they know if they don’t show up to school, I’m going to get on them,” said Henry.One of the kids taking the school-first approach is Michael Sanchez, whose dad signed him up for classes, but now he’s ready to take this sport as far as it can go.“I ended up liking it because I can learn from it, like discipline and hard work,” said Sanchez.

Before South Florida families sit down for Thanksgiving dinner, a local doctor says a few food safety precautions involving the turkey, kitchen and leftovers can help prevent an unwanted guest at the holiday table: food poisoning.WPTV's Michael Hoffman sat down with Dr. Kleper De Almeida an infectious disease specialist at Good Samaritan Medical Center to break down what people should know as they prepare Thanksgiving dinner and plan for the leftovers that follow."The concern is of salmonella," de Almeida said.His advice starts before the turkey ever reaches the oven.De Almeida told WPTV that a frozen turkey should be thawed in the refrigerator or using cold water.Keeping raw poultry from contaminating other ingredients and kitchen surfaces is an important part of the process.Current USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service guidance emphasizes keeping raw poultry separate from foods that will not be cooked and cleaning hands, utensils and surfaces throughout meal preparation. [fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida also cautioned against washing a raw turkey because water that touches the bird can contaminate the sink and surrounding areas."Heat from the cooking process is sufficient to kill the bacteria," de Almeida said. "Washing the bird is OK, but you have to keep in mind that the water that has touched the bird can contaminate the sink."When it comes to determining whether Thanksgiving turkey is safe to eat, temperature matters."Cooking the poultry at a temperature that exceeds 165 is sufficient to prevent the risk of salmonella infection and other infections," de Almeida said.The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service says turkey should reach a minimum internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, measured with a food thermometer in the thickest part of the breast, innermost part of the thigh and innermost part of the wing. [fsis.usda.gov]If stuffing is cooked inside the turkey, the center of the stuffing should also reach 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]Once Thanksgiving dinner is finished, food safety doesn't stop.Hoffman asked de Almeida how long people should keep digging into their Thanksgiving leftovers."Three days," de Almeida said. "So they have cooked the food on Thursday. They have Friday, Saturday, Sunday to get done with what was served."For additional context, federal food safety guidance gives a slightly broader window. The USDA advises refrigerating perishable leftovers within two hours and eating or freezing refrigerated Thanksgiving leftovers within three to four days. That makes the Monday after Thanksgiving the federal guidance's use-or-freeze deadline. [foodsafety.gov], [fsis.usda.gov]Leftovers should be reheated to an internal temperature of 165 degrees. [fsis.usda.gov]De Almeida advised people who are pregnant or immunocompromised to be particularly cautious with Thanksgiving leftovers."Women who are pregnant and immunocompromised people, they need to be extra cautious," de Almeida said. "And the rules for leftovers are more stringent, so they should consume the leftovers within one day."Food safety is especially important when preparing a large holiday meal with multiple dishes moving in and out of the refrigerator, oven and serving area.So while Thanksgiving is about good food, family and friends, keeping an eye on how that food is prepared, cooked, and stored can help ensure the holiday memories don't include a bout of food poisoning.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. New police body-camera video shows officers taking a man into custody after a 19-year-old woman reported being attacked along Boca Raton’s El Rio Trail. Now, people who frequent the trail say the attack, along with an earlier incident involving the same suspect at the same location, is making them reconsider their safety and call for a greater police presence.WATCH: El Rio Trail assault arrest caught on bodycam amid safety concernsBodycam shows suspect being taken into custodyPolice body-camera video shows officers taking 36-year-old LaPaul Jackson of Miami Gardens into custody following Monday’s attack.According to a Boca Raton police report, the 19-year-old woman was walking along El Rio Trail around 11:30 a.m. when Jackson allegedly approached her from behind with a knife and forced her into a wooded area.Police said the woman was attacked before she managed to escape and return to the trail, where someone helped her call 911. Investigators said she suffered multiple cuts.Police used the location of the woman’s stolen cellphone to track Jackson to a Palm Tran bus, according to the police affidavit.Jackson faces seven charges, including kidnapping, sexual battery with a deadly weapon, robbery with a weapon and tampering with a victim. Police records also show he is accused of violating his pretrial release in connection with an August robbery case.Attack raises safety concerns along El Rio TrailPeople who regularly walk and exercise along El Rio Trail told WPTV the daytime attack has changed how they think about their safety.“In shock, especially because it happened so early in the morning,” Isabel Chambers told WPTV.Luiz Souza said he was disappointed and believes more attention needs to be paid to the area.“Disappointment because the police is supposed to take care a little better of this place,” Souza said.Another person said the attack will make her reconsider walking the trail by herself.“Well, I’m going to think twice now about going alone,” she said.Previous incident adds to concernsThe concerns come as WPTV learned Jackson had previously been arrested in connection with another incident at the same location on El Rio Trail.According to police records, Jackson allegedly pushed a woman to the ground and stole her cellphone during an Aug. 1 incident. The affidavit says Jackson was on pretrial release in that case when the November incident occurred.Marvin Montoya told WPTV in Spanish that learning about the incidents caught him by surprise.“It surprises me, and I feel bad because if he hurt a woman or a young girl, he could hurt anyone,” Montoya said.Montoya added that he was glad Jackson was in custody.Calls for more police presenceWPTV asked Boca Raton police about the wooded encampment near the trail where investigators said Monday’s attack continued.Police said the property is privately owned, which presents an enforcement challenge because officers cannot enter simply to issue trespass warnings. Police confirmed previous arrests have been made in the area.Following the two incidents, people WPTV spoke with said they would like to see a more visible police presence along El Rio Trail.“It’d be nice to know that there’s somebody keeping an eye out for people,” one person said.More details from police recordsThe police affidavit provides additional details about how investigators tracked down Jackson.Police said the woman’s stolen iPhone had Life360 enabled, allowing her mother to provide officers with live location information. Investigators followed the phone’s movement to a Palm Tran bus near Northeast 20th Street and North Federal Highway.Officers found Jackson on the bus, according to the affidavit. Police also reported recovering the woman’s cellphone from the rear of the bus.Investigators said they recovered a large green serrated knife near El Rio Trail that the woman identified as the weapon used during the attack.According to the affidavit, officers also found a backpack in Jackson’s possession containing items including zip ties, duct tape, masks and a dark-colored long-sleeve jacket.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. An attorney for the developer behind the controversial Project Tango data center warned Palm Beach County of "significant and potentially catastrophic financial liability" if an expansion wasn't approved, according to a 180-page letter obtained by WPTV's Michael Hoffman. Ten days after the letter was sent, Palm Beach County zoning staff approved the expansion.The letter represents a new development in WPTV's nearly yearlong coverage of Project Tango and raises new questions about the October decision that allowed the project to triple its data center space without another vote by county commissioners.In July, Palm Beach County commissioners denied a separate proposal to expand the project. Then in October, county staff administratively approved another expansion.The letter from Project Tango attorney Ethan Loeb was sent before that October approval and threatened significant legal action if county staff did not approve the expansion.The 180-page letter included legal threats against Palm Beach County and a personal threat of legal action against county Zoning Director Wendy Hernandez.According to the letter, denying the expansion could result in "significant and potentially catastrophic financial liability."The letter went further, contending potential damages involving PBA Holdings could be "so significant that it would be impossible for the county to financially sustain the damages that PBA Holdings would recover."Ten days later, zoning staff approved the expansion.Hoffman spoke with District 6 Commissioner Katherine Waldron, who represents the area where the project would be located.Waldron said she believes the letter's threat against a county employee calls the approval process into question."That letter comes out threatening not just the county, but to one of our zoning people, and I think that that corrupts the process, and we should consider overturning the decision because of that," Waldron said.Among the issues raised in the letter were additional requirements placed on Project Tango, including continuous sound studies and real-time public noise monitoring.The letter accused Palm Beach County of never imposing those requirements on another property owner in the county's history.The project's potential noise and other impacts have been closely watched by people living near the proposed data center."It was shocking to say the very least," Arden resident Janice Ridenour said of the letter.Ridenour lives near the data center property and has been outspoken about Project Tango since it was announced.She helped spearhead the western communities' fight against the earlier Project Tango expansion that commissioners Vice President JD Vance and Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are preparing to meet, the incoming Democratic lawmaker and the White House said, after a bitter campaign season that featured sharp and at-times personal attacks between the two men.The circumstances of the would-be meeting were not immediately clear, nor was it certain on whose initiative it was being set. And Vance will ultimately preside over El-Sayed’s swearing-in Jan. 3. El-Sayed said in a Tuesday interview on MSNOW that his team was contacted by Vance's office for a meeting. Vance’s office said Wednesday that it had contacted El-Sayed’s staff after being told the Democrat sought time with the vice president.RELATED STORY | Democrat Abdul El-Sayed projected to win Michigan Senate raceThe talk of a meeting comes as Vance nears a decision on whether to seek the Republican nomination for the White House in 2028, which has been complicated by voters' bruising rejection of President Donald Trump in this month's midterm elections, and as El-Sayed prepares to take office as the nation’s first Muslim senator.Both men have in recent days expressed willingness to attempt to find common ground after their heated criticism — albeit on their own terms. Vance described El-Sayed as “very, very evil" while campaigning for Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers outside Detroit in August and appeared to question the Democrat's patriotism.Vance, however, sounded a much more charitable tone about the incoming Michigan senator during a Fox News Channel interview Monday.“If Abdul El-Sayed wants to work with me and the president to make people’s lives better, he’s going to find us very much a willing partner,” Vance said during the Fox segment.It was far from clear how and on what issues the two might cooperate, especially in light of El-Sayed's chief policy objective, a Medicare for All healthcare system the Trump administration, including Vance individually, has dismissed.RELATED STORY | Blue Jays distance team from Santander posts after El-Sayed’s Senate victoryBut it appeared at least to represent a rare bipartisan olive branch for President Donald Trump's attack dog in the wake of midterm elections, when Republicans were routed nationally while losing majorities in both houses of Congress, and as Vance looks ahead to his own future.“If he wants to work with us to get money out of politics, put money in pockets and pass Medicare for All, which is what I ran on, I'm a willing partner,” El-Sayed said on MS NOW.

House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018.The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.The Democrats’ majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.“Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure,” said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Mary Peltola projected to flip Alaska Senate seat, giving Democrats 56-44 majority“There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."Election rout creates a mandate to governThe numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans’ Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.She called the big numbers "a mandate for change.”Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.“Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it’s affecting the people,” he said.For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: “How does that affect people’s pocketbooks?”IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Democrats are most excited to support three candidates for 2028The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to “blatant criminality.”A new generation of leadersAfter House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority — meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition."We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK,” said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families,” Jordan said.The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

New research shows Florida law enforcement agencies could earn more than $1 billion in federal funding through next year for helping the Department of Homeland Security with immigration enforcement operations — far beyond what any other state could receive for its participation.Since February 2025, every law enforcement agency in Florida is required to have a 287(g) agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The agreement allows state and local law enforcement officers to conduct immigration enforcement activities on ICE's behalf. The 287(g) program has been around for 30 years.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "(It's) basically a program that if someone came into the jail, then the jail could run their information through an immigration database and alert ICE if they had an immigration detainer or some civil immigration issue, and then ICE could come and pick them up," said Felicity Rose, vice president of research and policy at fwd.us, a bipartisan advocacy organization that focuses on immigration and criminal justice. Rose and her team have been tracking the Trump administration's use of 287(g) agreements. They recently published a report using public and leaked records to estimate how much money local law enforcement agencies are getting from ICE in exchange for participating in 287(g)."Those partnerships are both sending billions of dollars to state and local law enforcement with very little oversight," Rose said.I asked Rose for her data on each sheriff's office in our five-county viewing area. In Palm Beach County, the report estimates more than $16 million in available funding for fiscal year 2026. In Martin County, the estimate is nearly $1.8 million, along with $5.3 million in St. Lucie County, $1.7 million in Okeechobee County and $880,000 in Indian River County.PREVIOUS COVERAGE: Several local police departments are enrolled in 287(g) program"After the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act in the summer of 2025 passed, they gave $191 billion to (the U.S. Department of Homeland Security). One thing they decided to do with that was start paying people who signed up for the task force model," Rose explained.ICE breaks down its 287(g) task force payment structure on its website: initial stipends of $100,000, plus $7,500 per credentialed officer. Then, quarterly stipends of $15,000 per officer per quarter. That's on top of salary reimbursement for officers' time working immigration enforcement, plus "quarterly monetary performance awards based on the successful location of illegal aliens.""That money led to a major change in the number of agencies signing up and, very importantly, the number of arrests that they were making," Rose said.The Florida Department of Law Enforcement tracks 287(g) arrests throughout the state. Their data states that since August 2025, the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office had 361, the Okeechobee County Sheriff's Office carried out 37, Indian River County had 38 and St. Lucie County had 15. The Martin County Sheriff's Office had 1,095 287(g) arrests.The Martin County Sheriff's Office declined an interview for this story, but Sheriff John Budensiek spoke to us in December 2025 about accepting funding to help with immigration detention."I don't think our taxpayers should be taxed again. I think the federal government, if they're going to use us as a tool, should pay for their portion of that," Budensiek said.A spokeswoman for MCSO told me in a statement that "The Martin County Sheriff's Office has not conducted any recent immigration enforcement operations under the 287(g) program. Individuals without lawful immigration status who are arrested on local criminal charges in Martin County are booked into the Martin County Jail. The number of those bookings is substantially lower than the figure you cited."Mariana Blanco and her team at the Guatemalan Maya Center in Lake Worth Beach have also been tracking immigration arrests and working with the families impacted by them."When you begin monetizing these arrests, now you lose sight of the protection of the people, and that's exactly what we're seeing," Blanco said.She tells me she's noticed a change in how and where those arrests have happened in recent months in Palm Beach County."So they're not just taking the driver in the vehicle; they're taking the passengers as well," Blanco said."When (people) called to report crimes, (deputies) have been arresting them because of their — due to their immigration status," Blanco said.I asked her if the person who called to report the crime gets arrested, and she confirmed that they do.I asked Blanco whether she worries about the impact that will have on crime overall in Lake Worth."Crime has been heavily under-reported in Lake Worth and I know that because PBSO has asked us for help in ... giving a sense of security for the people to report crimes," Blanco said. "We said, well, respectfully, we don't trust you, and so how would we tell the people that they could trust you?" The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office didn't respond to my requests for comment.The fwd.us report estimates law enforcement agencies across Florida could be eligible for a total of up to $1.4 billion through fiscal year 2027 from the federal government. The report also estimates that Florida has deputized 9,021 law enforcement officers under the 287(g) task force model and conducted 15,164 arrests since January 2025.To compare, the report shows Texas, the state believed to be eligible for the second-highest payday through 287(g), is estimated to qualify for roughly $421 million through FY 2027. The state is estimated to have deputized 4,082 officers and conducted 9,138 arrests through the program (although Rose noted that Florida provides more data on 287(g) than other states).I filed public records requests with our five local sheriff's offices to see how they were spending that money, beyond reimbursement for deputies' time. Those requests are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A Hillsborough County judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit challenging the way drivers' ticket appeals are handled for Florida's controversial school bus cameras — and the attorneys behind the case now want it to move forward on behalf of potentially thousands of other drivers.WATCH: Judge allows Hillsborough school bus camera lawsuit to proceedThe school bus stop arm cameras are designed to protect kids getting on and off school buses. But since they started rolling, Investigative Reporter Katie LaGrone and photojournalist Matthew Apthorp have exposed problems with what happens when drivers get a ticket and try to fight back.Stanley Shultz of Plant City was fined $225 last year after a school bus camera caught him passing the bus after its stop arm deployed. He said the bus' warning lights never flashed.So Shultz tried to challenge his violation — and lost — bringing his total fine to $270. But he's not done fighting, and neither is his attorney. "He challenged the merits of the ticket. We're challenging the procedure," said Shultz's attorney Gino Moreno.At issue: When a driver challenges one of these violations, who decides if it should be upheld or dismissed?Florida law calls for a "local hearing officer" appointed by the school district or county. But in Hillsborough County, contested cases are being sent to state administrative judges through the Division of Administrative Hearings — or DOAH — and in most of these cases, the judges aren't in the same county where the ticket was issued.In Shultz's appeal, the judge who heard his appeal was in Tallahassee. And that's against the law, according to Shultz's lawsuit."If you're saying that it has to be heard by a local hearing officer, the hearing officer is being described as local. A state agency in Tallahassee is not local," Moreno said.The Hillsborough County School District and its camera vendor, BusPatrol, tried to get the case dismissed. But recently, a judge said no, giving the green light for this camera lawsuit to keep rolling.Shultz's attorneys are now asking the court to certify the case as a class action, since there are thousands of other drivers in Hillsborough County whose appeals were also heard by judges outside the county.As of Oct. 2, nearly 5,000 school bus violations issued in Hillsborough County were contested — with nearly 80% upheld by a DOAH judge, according to recent data provided by the Hillsborough County School District.Last year, one of those judges revealed to Reporter LaGrone why the law makes it difficult for drivers to win appeals."It doesn't give us any discretion do anything but uphold the citation or void the citation," Judge John Van Laningham told LaGrone last year. For nearly two years, LaGrone and Apthorp have exposed problems with these cameras, which have generated nearly $30 million in paid fines in Hillsborough County alone.First, they discovered drivers were getting ticketed without a way to contest their fine. Then lawmakers had to adjust the law just to ensure drivers could appeal.It could take several months before a judge determines whether to certify this lawsuit as a class action. While this court battle is based in Hillsborough County, Moreno could expand the lawsuit to other Florida counties where DOAH judges are also being used to hear driver appeals.BusPatrol did not respond to our request for comment about this latest ruling but a spokesperson previously called the lawsuit "baseless." A spokesperson for the Hillsborough County school district said it does not comment on pending litigation. Shultz's attorney calls the lawsuit necessary for drivers to get a fair shot at fighting back what these buses capture on camera."You opened up this program before you set up a hearing program, then you changed the law, and then you still can't follow the law. That's ultimately what our position is: just get it right," Moreno said.

Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance.Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives.Watch more from Kate Hussey:In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding.But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending."We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it."The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts.Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible.Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames.For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming."It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview.For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes."Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said.But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced."We are fully gutted. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone."Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost.And not everyone will qualify."You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said.That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation.Martin County estimates the flooding caused:$14 million in beach damage.Nearly $1 million in damaged roads requiring repaving.$3 million in residential losses.Additional expenses associated with county staff overtime and emergency response.A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents.But approval is not guaranteed.When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management.Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request."If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked.Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials."This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well."He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs.In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents.Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens.Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own."There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting.Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks.But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified."Well, that would be ... we'd have to talk to staff," he said.County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed."They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey.Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs.Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup."We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said.That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth."We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said.However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance.The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners.Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed.County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources.Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers.Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs."We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said."As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted."The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding."Please. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners.Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers."And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked.Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process."I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said.Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward.But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance.As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida.According to Perdue, Gov. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties.The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies."We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said.The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted.Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance."We're committed. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet."Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved.FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied.For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding.It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in."This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

A Russian national pleaded guilty Friday to his role in a Medicare fraud scheme rooted in Palm Beach County, marking the first conviction in a case I first brought to you last year.In federal court, 29-year-old Nika Machutadze, with the help of a translator, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering. He is one of the defendants linked to a fraudulent medical equipment company in Delray Beach called Sunshine Senior Solutions, and he admitted under oath to his involvement in a money laundering scheme totaling more than $7 million.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Machutadze could face up to 20 years in prison, plus fines, restitution and deportation.Seniors first contacted me last year, sharing Medicare statements for medical equipment they didn't need — or receive — from Sunshine Senior Solutions.While I tallied up hundreds of thousands of dollars in false claims from the statements I reviewed, that was a drop in the bucket, according to federal prosecutors. Federal prosecutors say Sunshine Senior Solutions billed insurers for more than $3 billion, though only a fraction of that was paid out. Machutadze admitted to opening bank accounts for Sunshine Senior Solutions and a second similar business in Texas, and transferring some of the money paid by insurers overseas.I reached out to some of the seniors to share the news of the guilty plea."Oh, that's terrific," said Laura Carmine, of Illinois. "Nice to know that justice can be done.""I'm glad to hear that," said Mike Parrett, of Ohio.I spoke with Machutadze's attorney, Tony Mirvis, after Friday's hearing."The government's evidence was overwhelming," Mirvis said. Mirvis said his client thought he was just taking a job."What I think is important is he's like the tip of the spear," Mirvis said. "I hate to say it, but he's kind of like a victim because the people that got him to work— they're the ones that are making the millions of dollars, and he's making like literally nothing. He's getting in trouble for it."Information filed in Friday's case mentions another defendant, Ibrahim Hilmi, and a second, unnamed co-conspirator. Hilmi, who is also tied to Sunshine Senior Solutions, is scheduled for trial in February."Everybody that's involved with this should get prosecuted, and they should get punished for what they did," Mirvis said.Mirvis told me his client will not be cooperating with federal investigators on any other prosecutions.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Democrat Eileen Laubacher has defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado's 4th Congressional District, according to a race call by The Associated Press more than a week after Election Day.The race remained too close to call for days as election officials continued counting ballots. Laubacher's victory unseats one of President Donald Trump's most outspoken allies in Congress. Boebert has represented Colorado's 4th Congressional District since 2025. She previously represented the state's 3rd Congressional District but switched districts in late 2023, citing the need for a "fresh start following a difficult year" that included family turmoil and several controversies.Laubacher, a retired Navy admiral who served in the military for more than 30 years, said her decision to run for Congress was driven by concerns about the country's future."I have never felt as much of a threat to our country, our Constitution, our very democracy, as I do at this time," Laubacher said.

Sullivan, a military veteran seeking a third term, received support from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.Sullivan aligned his campaign with the Trump administration's tax and spending priorities and advocated for expanding fossil fuel production.The race in Alaska was complicated by the presence of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot. Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, ran as a long shot Democratic candidate for Senate. Both Dan Sullivans running prompted a legal fight early in the campaign, and President Donald Trump later called the former teacher's campaign "fake" and "a hoax by the Democrats."

Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, are in custody after the Martin County Sheriff's Office says a 17-year-old heard a suspicious noise outside his family's home in Palm City's Evergreen Club, prompting a 911 call and an extensive overnight search. Investigators say the group parked a vehicle near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community and targeting a home. Deputies later recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm during their investigation.WATCH: Teen's Alert Leads to 4 Arrests After Palm City ManhuntThe sheriff's office is now asking residents in the Evergreen Club community to check their homes, vehicles and security cameras for anything suspicious as investigators try to determine why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Martin County and whether any other properties were targeted.Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when the family's 17-year-old son realized something was wrong."The 17-year-old son heard a noise, woke up, knew something was wrong, but didn't quite know what it was," Budensiek said. "(He) went and talked to his parents."The family then began reviewing footage from security cameras around the property.According to Budensiek, one camera was no longer working properly. When the family went farther back through the recorded footage, he said they discovered people moving around the home."They could see that one of their cameras wasn't working," Budensiek said. "They kept going further back in their search history, and saw where these three black males actually were circling the house."Budensiek said the video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door so activity there could no longer be seen.The family called 911.Deputies began searching the area outside the gated community and checked a parking lot near the C-23 Canal."There indeed was a car parked there," Budensiek said.The sheriff's office said the suspects had parked along the canal before walking into the neighborhood.One person was taken into custody near the vehicle, while the others fled, according to the sheriff.Deputies established a perimeter and searched with assistance from aviation and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Budensiek said two of the people who fled were ultimately discovered hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal."Two fled and ended up hiding under the bridge that crosses the C-23 Canal on Murphy Road," Budensiek said. "They were the last two to actually be apprehended after an extensive manhunt."The three adults arrested were identified as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson. A 16-year-old was also arrested, but WPTV is not identifying the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to published reports citing the sheriff's office. Wise also faces grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. As investigators retraced the route between the suspects' vehicle and the family's home, Budensiek said they recovered a handgun."They recovered a handgun that was stolen with an extended magazine, and were able to corroborate again what the intended victim said," Budensiek said.The Sheriff's Office has also reported recovering masks and gloves during the investigation. Investigators are now trying to determine why this particular home may have been targeted."We don't know why that house," Budensiek said. "We don't know if they went to any other houses potentially in the middle of the night."The sheriff's office is asking residents to review their security footage and inspect their homes and vehicles for missing property or possible evidence of another attempted break-in.Anyone who discovers missing property or signs of a break-in is asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.Investigators are also examining digital evidence as they work to establish why the four made the trip from Jacksonville to Palm City.MORE PALM CITY: Judge rejects motion to dismiss animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki CamerlengoThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A St. Lucie County woman, who had told investigators she was trying to exorcise demons from her son's body, has been declared unfit to stand trial in his death.Court records show that Rhonda Paulynice was committed to the Department of Children and Families to see if her competency can be restored. A homeowner's quick call to 911 helped interrupt an attempted home invasion in Palm City early Tuesday, leading to the arrests of four people from Jacksonville, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.The sheriff's office said the homeowner heard a noise outside a home on Southwest Bimini Circle in the Evergreen Club and contacted authorities. Deputies established a perimeter and, with assistance from the agency's aviation, drone and K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department K-9 unit, found all four hiding in separate locations throughout the community.Investigators believe the group parked near a canal and walked into the neighborhood to target the home. Deputies said they recovered a firearm, masks and gloves. Detectives later determined the gun had been reported stolen.The sheriff's office identified three of those arrested as 21-year-old Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., 21-year-old Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and 21-year-old Cameron Elijah Mapson.
