WPTV is not naming the juvenile.All four face attempted home invasion charges and were taken into custody, according to the sheriff's office.Wise also faces charges of grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.The sheriff's office credited the homeowner's quick decision to call authorities with interrupting the alleged crime before anyone was hurt.

A Port St. Lucie man has been sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison for using artificial intelligence to impersonate a popular online streamer as part of a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that authorities say cost victims about $260,000.David Anthony Sanchez, 36, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison after pleading guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.Federal prosecutors said Sanchez, who also went by "Dave the Jewler," "Rueben Alexis De Jesus Santana" and other aliases, impersonated online streamer N3ON to convince organizers of a cryptocurrency memecoin project that the streamer had agreed to endorse and participate in it.According to court records, Sanchez created online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3ON and communicated with the project's organizers while posing as both the streamer and his representative.Prosecutors said Sanchez also executed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent organizers an AI-generated voice recording that mimicked the streamer's voice to falsely confirm his participation.Believing the representations were legitimate, the victims transferred approximately $260,000 in cryptocurrency to accounts controlled by Sanchez, according to prosecutors.Authorities said Sanchez later converted a substantial portion of the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to conceal the source and ownership of the money. Prosecutors said he used the proceeds for his personal benefit."Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm," Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in the release. She said Sanchez exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate victims' trust and take their money.In addition to his 47-month prison sentence, Sanchez was ordered to pay restitution to the victims. The amount of restitution was not specified in the release.The FBI's Miami Field Office investigated the case.

Nearly 1.8 million chickens will be depopulated after highly pathogenic avian influenza, commonly known as bird flu, was detected at a Cal-Maine Foods facility in Okeechobee County.Cal-Maine Foods announced Nov. 18 that the facility tested positive for highly pathogenic avian influenza, or HPAI. The company said the outbreak will lead to the depopulation of approximately 1.4 million laying hens and 360,000 pullets, representing about 2.7% of the company's total flock.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Production at the Okeechobee County facility has temporarily stopped while Cal-Maine follows protocols established by the U.S. Department of Agriculture.The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services has established a quarantine area following the detection, according to St. Lucie County government.The poultry quarantine extends from Okeechobee County into a rural portion of western St. Lucie County north of State Road 70 near the county line.People who own or care for poultry within the affected area are being advised to review the state's quarantine restrictions, which include limits on moving poultry and poultry products without FDACS authorization. Residents can check whether they are within the affected area using the state's interactive quarantine map.Cal-Maine said it is coordinating production and distribution among its other facilities in an effort to maintain its egg supply and minimize disruptions for customers.The company also said it maintains biosecurity programs at its facilities but noted that no farm is immune to HPAI. The virus remains present among wild birds, and the risk of outbreaks can increase during bird migration seasons.Health officials say the detection does not mean consumers should stop eating eggs. According to information provided by the company, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers the health risk from HPAI viruses to the general U.S. public to be low.The USDA also says HPAI is not transmitted through properly handled and cooked eggs. Cal-Maine said there is no known HPAI risk associated with eggs currently on the market and that no eggs have been recalled because of the outbreak.Cal-Maine said it is working with federal, state and local officials as it responds to the outbreak and works to reduce the risk of additional infections.The company said it expects to provide more information in its next quarterly report filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission and does not anticipate providing interim updates unless information is considered material.Anyone with questions about the quarantine can contact FDACS at 850-410-0900 or find additional information through its Division of Animal Industry.

The sound of bagpipes and taps filled the air Saturday as the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a new memorial honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty.The memorial, located outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building, honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Their deaths happened 40 years apart. Now, their names have a permanent place together.WATCH: New memorial honors two Indian River County deputies killed in line of dutyThe unveiling came exactly one year after Sweeting-Mashkow was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community.47-year-old Sweeting-Mashkow was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said 37-year-old Michael Halberstam retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder.A locksmith who was there for the eviction, David Long, was also critically wounded and later died from his injuries.Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death marked the second line-of-duty death in the 100-year history of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office.For those who gathered Saturday, the passage of a year has not made that loss feel distant.“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”The memorial also reaches back four decades, honoring Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.“The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for Saturday’s unveiling, paying their respects.“I am so glad that they did this for Terri and Raczkoski,” one community member said.For those at the ceremony, the memorial is also a reminder of the risks law enforcement officers face each time they go to work.“All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” says Knott.Flowers hopes the two names on the memorial will be the only ones it ever bears: “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again."

A Port St. Lucie family says it has spent nearly four years trying to get a swale liner installed to keep stagnant water from lingering in its yard, a problem the family says leaves water sitting for days and turns the property into what they jokingly call a "mosquito hotel."Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, brought the problem to WPTV's Michael Hoffman after meeting him at WPTV's Let's Hear It community meetup in Jensen Beach.Their frustration centers on a yearslong wait and changing rules over who is responsible for installing the swale liner. Now, the city says the family is not alone and that it recently received approval to add a contractor to help speed up installations.Fasulo and Todd told Hoffman their problem dates back to when their Port St. Lucie home was built.At the time, the city was changing its rules surrounding responsibility for installing swale liners, which are designed to help keep water moving rather than allowing it to remain on properties.According to the family, installation had been the city's responsibility before shifting to builders. It has since shifted back to the city.Their house, they said, was built between those changes and never received one.The family eventually contacted Port St. Lucie."They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it," Fasulo said.Fasulo said she understood that requirement. What frustrated her was how long her family was told it would take."I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done," she said.Now, Fasulo said the family has been told it could take another two years.That's when they turned to WPTV."We've seen you guys get results," Fasulo told Hoffman.The family provided WPTV with pictures showing water collecting around the property even after lighter rainfall.They also walked Hoffman around their property to show him the problem firsthand.The standing water wasn't the only issue they encountered. Mosquitoes quickly made their presence known.Fasulo has a name for it."Mosquito hotel," she said.For the family, however, the nickname highlights a problem they've been trying to resolve for years: Water takes days to clear from their property, and they say they cannot install the needed liner themselves.Hoffman brought the family's concerns to the city and sat down with Scott Samples to ask why the process has taken so long and what is being done about it.Samples said the family is not the only one waiting."We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in," Samples said.The city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to address the outstanding installations more quickly, Samples told WPTV."We're looking at, again, how can we maximize the resources that we have available to help the residents as quickly as we can, knowing that we're limited," Samples said. "You know, so we try to put this, there's plans, and then you have to adjust those plans as you go as well. So we're sort of in that process right now."For Fasulo and Todd, that still does not provide a date for when their swale liner will finally be installed.But after nearly four years of waiting, they now have WPTV asking those questions alongside them."You guys have helped in the past with this issue," Fasulo said. "So we decided to ask you guys to help us and whoever else is in need and not getting answers from the city."WPTV will continue following the family's case and pressing Port St. Lucie for updates on when the work will be completed.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval.WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data centerOn Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95.They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. Friday.At 4:55 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent."We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said.Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project.But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development.Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application.On Oct. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations.But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

It's about inspiring the community, creating opportunities and showing the world that with determination and a clear vision, anything is possible. We're making history together, and we're just getting started. Why dream when you can live it?"FIU’s athletics director Scott Carr also commented on the partnership with the rapper, whose full name is Armando Christian Perez."This is a historic day for FIU Athletics to uniquely partner with a world-renowned artist and amazing person who truly values relationships and his community," Carr said in a press release. "Armando's financial support is program-changing, but him providing a microphone to amplify FIU will be even more beneficial to growing our brand. I couldn't be more excited about our partnership as this will take us to another level. We can now officially say: 'Paws Up, Dale!'"Van Wagner College, a third-party multimedia rights partner with FIU Athletics since 2016, assisted in the deal. The school helped secure additional partners, such as South Dade Kia, which FIU said will be the presenting sponsor of the field — South Dade Kia Field at Pitbull Stadium.No stranger to the education space, Pitbull also founded the first tuition-free public charter SLAM! school — for sports leadership, arts and management — in Miami in 2012.

France’s high-speed rail network was hit Friday with widespread and “criminal” acts of vandalism including arson attacks, paralyzing travel to Paris from across the rest of France and Europe only hours before the grand opening ceremony of the Olympics.French officials condemned the attacks as “criminal actions,” though they said there was no sign of a direct link to the Games, and prosecutors in Paris opened a national investigation saying the crimes could carry sentences of 15 to 20 years.As Paris authorities geared up for a spectacular parade on and along the Seine River, three fires were reported near the tracks on the high-speed lines of Atlantique, Nord and Est, causing disruptions that affected hundreds of thousands of travelers.Among them were two German athletes in showjumping who were on a train to Paris to take part in the opening ceremony but had to turn back in Belgium because of the closures, and will now miss the ceremony, German news agency dpa reported.“There was no longer a chance of making it on time,” rider Philipp Weishaupt, who was traveling with teammate Christian Kukuk, told dpa.French Prime Minister Gabriel Attal wrote on the social media platform X that France’s intelligence services have been mobilized to find the perpetrators.Attal characterized them as “acts of sabotage,” which were “prepared and coordinated.”There were no known reports of injuries.RELATED STORY | Previewing the Paris Summer Olympics: When does it start, how to watchTransport Minister Patrice Vergriete described people fleeing from the scene of fires and the discovery of incendiary devices. “Everything indicates that these are criminal fires,” he said.The incidents paralyzed several high-speed lines linking Paris to the rest of France and to neighboring countries, Vergriete said, speaking on BFM television.The French national rail company SNCF said that areas affecting rail track intersections were targeted to double the impact.“For one fire, two destinations were hit,” the company's CEO, Jean-Pierre Farandou.It was “a premeditated, calculated, coordinated attack" that indicates "a desire to seriously harm” the French people, Farandou said.The attack occurred against a backdrop of global tensions and heightened security measures as the city prepared for the 2024 Olympic Games. Many travelers were planning to converge on the capital for the opening ceremony, and many vacationers were also in transit.French authorities have foiled several plots to disrupt the Olympics, including arresting a Russian man on suspicion of planning to destabilize the games.The Paris police prefecture “concentrated its personnel in Parisian train stations” after the “massive attack” that paralyzed the TGV high-speed network, Laurent Nuñez, the Paris police chief, told France Info television.RELATED STORY | Olympic soccer gets off to violent and chaotic start as Morocco fans rush the field vs ArgentinaAlso Friday, the French airport of Basel-Mulhouse on the border with Germany and Switzerland was evacuated in the morning and remained temporarily closed “for safety reasons," the airport said. It wasn't clear whether there was a connection to the rail attacks.The disruptions hit Paris’ Montparnasse station particular hard.In the station's crowded hall, Maiwenn Labbé-Sorin said she spent hours stranded on a train before it doubled back to Paris.“We stayed two hours without water, without toilets, without electricity," she said. "Then we could go out on the track for a bit and then the train returned. Now I’m not sure what’s going to happen.”Many passengers at the Gare du Nord, one of Europe’s busiest train stations, were looking for answers and solutions on Friday morning. All eyes were on the central message boards as most services to northern France, Belgium and the United Kingdom were delayed.“It’s a hell of a way to start the Olympics,” said Sarah Moseley, 42, as she learned that her train to London was an hour late.“They should have more information for tourists, especially if it’s a malicious attack,” said Corey Grainger, a 37-year-old Australian sales manager on his way to London, as he rested on his two suitcases in the middle of the station.Sports Minister Amélie Oudéa-Castera said authorities were working to “evaluate the impact on travelers, athletes, and ensure the transport of all delegations to the competition sites” for the Olympics. Speaking on BFM television, she added, “Playing against the Games is playing against France, against your own camp, against your country.”SNCF said it did not know when traffic would resume and feared that disruptions would continue “at least all weekend.” SNCF teams “were already on site to carry out diagnostics and begin repairs,” but the “situation should last at least all weekend while the repairs are carried out,” the operator said. SNCF advised “all passengers to postpone their journey and not to go to the station,” specifying in its press release that all tickets were exchangeable and refundable.Valerie Pecresse, president of the regional council of the greater Paris region, speaking from Montparnasse station, said “250,000 travelers will be affected today on all these lines.” Substitution plans were underway, but Pecresse advised travelers “not to go to stations.”The troubles comes ahead of an opening ceremony has been planned for later Friday, in which 7,000 Olympic athletes are due to sail down the Seine past iconic Parisian monuments such as Notre-Dame Cathedral, the Louvre Museum, and the Musee d’Orsay.

West Palm Beach native Markus Edegran is ready and hopeful to compete in his first Olympics.Markus will be competing in kite foiling. This combines kite boarding and foiling. Foiling is the latest technique to come into sailing.A foil is a type of board with an extended rudder. This allows the board to rise above the water and the sailor to move at much faster paces without the friction of the water along the board.When you achieve foiling, it is almost like you are flying over the water. Although it looks serene and peaceful, it is very difficult to achieve.Markus told us that it takes a lot of patience and balance to maintain the necessary foiling technique. He also explained that kite foiling goes at extreme paces, about 50 mph across the waters. He explained it best when he said that he can kite foil from Lake Worth Beach to the Juno Beach Pier faster than we can drive it.Markus explained to us what foiling means for the sport of sailing."The foiling is the way the sport is heading," Markus said. It's more exciting to sail. It's more exciting to watch. I think that half the classes are foiling classes. So yeah, super excited to be a part of that."He had an early introduction to the water as he followed his brothers’ footsteps and started sailing at 8 years old. He said there was a steep learning curve, but he was automatically hooked.I asked him about his emotions ahead of the games and he didn’t have much to say regarding those. Markus is very calm ahead of the games and is treating it just like any other five-day race."I'm super happy it all lined up and brought me here today," Markus said.He has been training in the Marseille waters off and on for the last three years ahead of the games. We are rooting for you Markus and hope you contribute to the USA medal count.Markus’ competition begins on Aug. 4.

Boca Raton native Caroline Marks from the United States won the women's surfing gold medal on Monday at the Paris Olympics in Tahiti, while French Polynesian Kauli Vaast won the gold medal in men’s surfing.Marks, 22, was born in Boca but grew up in Melbourne Beach in Brevard County.SPECIAL COVERAGE: 2024 Paris OlympicsCheers and tears erupted from boats floating near the wave and crowds of spectators along the shore as the men's final match ended in the afternoon. Vaast pumped his arms into the air in victory after beating Jack Robinson from Australia, who received the silver medal.“I don’t really realize it, but I just made history,” said Vaast. “I can’t be prouder to represent Tahiti and France at home.”The women's gold medal match ended about thirty minutes later, with Marks beating Tatiana Weston-Webb from Brazil, who was awarded the silver medal.“Your whole life goes into a moment like this,” Marks said with a gold medal hanging around her neck. “It’s beyond all my wildest dreams.”For the bronze medals, Gabriel Medina from Brazil and Johanne Defay from France won after beating Alonso Correa from Peru and Brisa Hennessy from Costa Rica, respectively.“Chopes gave me so many good waves, so many good results. So I can’t complain,” said Medina, using a common nickname for Teahupo'o.Medalists — some in bare feet — stepped on to the Olympic podium near the ocean as crowds gathered to cheer and take photographs. Roosters ran along the grass while young local surfers called the names of the athletes as they walked by.All winners of the Paris Olympics surfing competition are first-time Olympic medalists, after defending Olympic women’s champion Carissa Moore of the United States — who won at the Tokyo Games, where Olympic surfing debuted — was beaten in the quarterfinals on Thursday.“Obviously I’m really sad to not be a part of finals day, to get to represent my home and my family one more time, but I’m really grateful,” Moore said after her loss. “I just hope that at the end of the day I can encourage whoever is watching, win or lose, don’t be afraid to go into it fearlessly and don’t be afraid to fail.”The final day of the Paris Olympics surfing competition began Monday morning after two days of delays due to unfavorable conditions. In the morning, conditions were smaller than the heavy, barrel-shaped waves Teahupo’o is famed for and that were seen during part of the men’s competition the week before.But by the afternoon waves grew larger and more frequent, giving athletes a chance to impress judges with the time they spent inside the barrels. At one point during the competition a whale jumped out of the water while surfers went head to head.Six of the eight surfers who made it to the semifinals represented different nations. French Polynesian, Peruvian, Australian and other national flags flew from boats near the waves.While not every surfer who competed was able to bring home a medal, many agreed that the second-ever Olympics surfing competition — filled with viral photographs, record-breaking scores and hours of stunning video footage broadcast to viewers around the world — helped promote the sport."Everyone’s watching and paying attention,” said Medina, who said he gained millions of social media followers after a photo of him floating in the sky next to his surfboard while bailing out of a wave went viral during the competition.

Celebrating its reputation as a cradle of revolution, Paris kicked off its first Summer Olympics in a century on Friday with a rain-soaked, rule-breaking opening ceremony studded with stars and fantasy along the Seine River.On-and-off showers — the first rain at a Summer Olympics' opening ceremony in more than 70 years — did not seem to hamper the enthusiasm of the athletes. Some held umbrellas as they rode boats down the river in a showcase of the city’s resilience as authorities investigated suspected acts of sabotage targeting France's high-speed rail network.Widespread travel disruptions triggered by what French officials called coordinated arson attacks on high-speed rail lines as well as the weather had dampened the mood ahead of the ceremony.Still, crowds crammed the Seine's banks and bridges and watched from balconies, “oohing” and “aahing” as Olympic teams paraded in boats down the waterway that got increasingly choppy as the weather worsened.Undeterred from the festivities, many of the hundreds of thousands of spectators huddled under umbrellas, plastic ponchos or jackets as the rain intensified, others danced and sang, and some dashed from their seats for shelter.“The rain can't stop us,” said U.S. basketball star LeBron James, sporting a plastic poncho along with the other American flag bearer, tennis player Coco Gauff.The weather made for some bizarre scenes at the show combining prerecorded and live performances: a stiff upper-lipped pianist played on even as small puddles formed on his grand piano. A breakdancer flipped her moves on the sheen of a rain-drenched platform. Some athletes in Bermuda-style colorful shirts looked dressed for the beach, not a deluge.As global audiences tuned in, Paris put its best foot forward — quite literally, with a spectacular Olympic launch that lifted spirits and joyous French cancan dancers featured early on. A humorous short film featured soccer icon Zinedine Zidane. Plumes of French blue, white and red smoke followed.Lady Gaga sang in a prerecorded performance, in French, with dancers shaking pink plumed pompoms, injecting a cabaret feel. To close the show, Celine Dion, standing under the Eiffel Tower, belted out her first live performance since the French-Canadian singer was diagnosed with stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological disorder, at the end of 2022.French-Malian pop star Aya Nakamura, the most listened-to French-speaking artist in the world, emerged from a pyrotechnic display in an all-gold out to sing her hit “Djadja” accompanied by a Republican guard band of the French army.More than three hours into the show, French President Emmanuel Macron declared the Games open. In a gaffe shortly beforehand, the five-ring Olympic flag was raised upside down at the Trocadero across from the Eiffel Tower.The final torch relay spanned landmarks like the Louvre and included sports legends like tennis greats Serena Williams and Rafael Nadal before French judo champ Teddy Riner and three-time Olympic champion runner Marie-Jose Perec lit the Olympic cauldron attached to a giant balloon, which floated into the Paris night.The ceremony celebrated women, including 10 golden statues of female pioneers that rose from giant pedestals along the river. Among them was Olympe de Gouges, who drafted the Declaration of the Rights of Women and the Female Citizen in 1791 during the French Revolution. She campaigned for the abolition of slavery and was guillotined in 1793.The Paris Games aim to be the first with equal numbers of men and women competing.With the ambitious ceremony, the stakes for France were immense. Dozens of heads of state and government were in town, and the world was watching as Paris turned itself into a giant open-air theater. Along the Seine, iconic monuments became stages for dancers, singers and other artists.Sofia Cohen, 20, watching with her father, called the ceremony “electric.” The Nicaraguan-Americans said the roar of applause given to the Ukrainian team was their favorite part.“Every Olympics is different, and this one was very French. The ceremony started out very majestic and regal. And as the rain started pouring down and time went on, everything got a little more hectic and fun,” she said.The sprawling event gave organizers bigger crowds to transport, organize and safeguard than would have been the case if they’d followed the example of previous Olympic host cities that opened with stadium shows.Still, as the show got underway, optimism soared that Paris — true to its motto that speaks of being unsinkable — might just see its gambles pay off. That's despite the soggy weather — no other Summer Olympics opening ceremony has had rain since Helsinki in 1952.Paris organizers said 6,800 of the 10,500 athletes would attend before they embark on the next 16 days of competition.The boats carrying the Olympic teams started the parade by breaking through curtains of water that cascaded down from Austerlitz Bridge, the start of the 6-kilometer (nearly 4-mile) route. The jetting waters were a wink at the fountains of Versailles Palace, the venue for Olympic equestrian competitions.Per Olympic protocol, the first boat carried athletes from Greece, birthplace of the ancient Games. It was followed by the Olympic team of refugee athletes and then, the other nations in French alphabetical order.Usually during Olympic opening ceremonies, the parade of athletes takes place during a pause in the razzmatazz. But Paris shattered that tradition by having the parade and pageantry at the same time, blending sports and artistic expression.Some spectators who followed organizers’ advice to arrive well ahead of time along the ceremony route fumed over long waits to get to their seats.“Paris has been great, anything to do with the Olympics and dissemination of information has been horrible,” said Tony Gawne, a 54-year-old Texan who turned up six hours in advance with his wife.“When you spend $6,000 on two tickets, well, that’s a little frustrating,” he said.But Paris had plenty of aces up its sleeve. The Eiffel Tower, its head visible below the clouds, Notre Dame Cathedral — restored from the ashes of its 2019 fire — the Louvre Museum and other iconic monuments starred in the opening ceremony. Award-winning theater director Thomas Jolly, the show’s creative mind, was using the signature Paris cityscape of zinc-gray rooftops as the playground for his imagination.His task: Tell the story of France, its people, their history and essence in a way that leaves an indelible imprint on Olympic audiences. Refresh the image and self-confidence of the French capital that was repeatedly struck by deadly extremist attacks in 2015. Capture how Paris is also aiming to reboot the Olympics, with Summer Games it has worked to make more appealing and sustainable.It’s a big ask. So Paris went big, very big. That goes for the security, too. Large fenced-off stretches of central Paris were locked down to those without passes and the skies during the ceremony were a no-fly zone for 93 miles around.During the athletes’ waterborne adventure, they passed historic landmarks that have been temporarily transformed into arenas for Olympic sports.Concorde Plaza, where French revolutionaries guillotined King Louis XVI and other royals, now hosting skateboarding and other sports. The golden-domed resting place of Napoléon Bonaparte, the backdrop for Olympic archery, and the Eiffel Tower, which donated chunks of iron that have been inlaid in the gold, silver and bronze Olympic medals. They’ll be won in the 32 sports’ 329 medal events.Paris’ aim, said Estanguet, is “to show to the whole world and to all of the French that in this country, we’re capable of exceptional things.”

A hot topic amongst tourists and athletes at the 2024 Olympics is the decision France made to forgo including air conditioning in Olympic Village.Some countries have chosen to supply their own air conditioning units to their competitors, like Team USA. Other countries have agreed with France's decision and will not provide air conditioning to their athletes.Summertime in Paris is much more tolerable than you initially would think.The average high temperatures are in the mid 70s with overnight lows in the upper 50s and low 60s.Last year, Paris did deal with record-breaking heat as temperatures soared over 86 degrees.A key component to keeping the Olympic Village between 73 and 79 degrees is in the piping. Water pipes under the floor's surface will aid in keeping the village in more comfortable conditions without the aid of air conditioning units.This is all in an effort to make the 2024 Olympics the greenest yet.France has kept the goal of keeping carbon emissions at a minimum this year. You will notice most of the Olympic sporting venues are historic sites where they only had to construct grandstands and the competition ground, rather than building new Olympic structures.

Salt Lake City has officially been named the host city for the 2034 Winter Olympics.International Olympic Committee President Thomas Bach made the announcement during a livestreamed session Wednesday from Paris, where the Summer Olympics are gearing up.“The International Olympic Committee has the honor to announce that the 27th Winter Games 2034 are awarded to Salt Lake City, Utah,” Bach said.RELATED STORY | Previewing the Paris Summer Olympics: When does it start, how to watchCheers and applause erupted in the crowd, with a number of Utah officials in attendance.Salt Lake City previously hosted the Winter Olympics back in 2002, and its sports venues from then still exist.Utah Gov. Spencer Cox took the podium following the news, and thanked the IOC for its generosity.RELATED STORY | Coco Gauff named Team USA's youngest-ever flag bearer, joins Lebron James“Our commitment to you is that we will work to unify, not just the United States of America, but the entire world around sports again,” Cox said. “Our world needs the Olympic and Paralympic movement now more than ever, and we will make you proud.”“To the people celebrating back home — we're back, baby,” Cox said.The IOC also approved a bid for the French Alps to host the 2030 Winter Games on Wednesday, but that is tentative. There are conditions attached to the approval and whoever becomes the next prime minister of France will have to sign off on it.

Tennis star and Delray Beach native Coco Gauff will join LeBron James as a flag bearer for the U.S. Olympic team at Friday's opening ceremony.Gauff, the reigning U.S. Open champion, is set to make her Olympic debut at the Paris Games and will be the first tennis athlete to carry the U.S. flag. She and James were chosen by Team USA athletes.COMPLETE COVERAGE: 2024 Paris OlympicsThe 20-year-old Gauff made the American team for the Tokyo Games three years ago as a teenager but had to sit out those Olympics because she tested positive for COVID-19 right before she was supposed to fly to Japan.Now Gauff, who is based in Florida, is a Grand Slam title winner in singles and doubles. She won her first major championship in New York in September, defeating Aryna Sabalenka in the singles final of the U.S. Open, then added her first Grand Slam doubles trophy at the French Open this June alongside Katerina Siniakova of the Czech Republic.The same clay courts at Roland Garros used for the French Open will be where matches are going to be held for the Paris Olympics. The draw to set the brackets is Thursday, and play begins on Friday.Gauff is seeded No. 2 in singles, matching her current WTA ranking behind No. 1 Iga Swiatek of Poland, and will be among the medal favorites.She and her usual doubles partner, Jessica Pegula, are seeded No. 1 in women's doubles. It's possible Gauff could also be entered in mixed doubles, but those pairings have not been announced yet.

Coco Gauff came back to defeat Ons Jabeur 4-6, 6-2, 6-3 at the French Open on Tuesday to reach the semifinals at a third consecutive Grand Slam tournament.Gauff won her first major title at the U.S. Open in September, then made it to the final four at the Australian Open in January.The 20-year-old American is seeded No. 3 at Roland Garros, where she was the runner-up to Iga Swiatek in 2022.Gauff could get a rematch in the semifinals against the top-ranked Swiatek, who has won three of the past four titles in Paris.Swiatek’s quarterfinal against 2023 Wimbledon champion Marketa Vondrousova was scheduled for later Tuesday on Court Philippe Chatrier.Jabeur's mix of speeds and spins gave Gauff fits at times. And as well-known as Gauff is for her ability to cover the court and play defense, Jabeur managed to keep coming up with winners, finishing with 30 in all.“She was playing really well the whole match. She was hitting a lot of winners on me, which is something I’m not used to against anybody,” Gauff said. “So today I was just trying to just be aggressive toward the end.”Gauff pulled away to a 5-2 lead in the last set, then needed a trio of match points to close things out, acknowledging afterward that maybe she grew a little tight down the stretch. The last game was key, with Gauff needing to save a break point, then Jabeur dismissing one match point with a disguised drop shot that earned a roar from the stands that the 29-year-old Tunisian responded to by putting her right index finger to her ear.But on Gauff's next opportunity to seal the victory, Jabeur badly flubbed an overhead. Gauff smiled, then raised her arms and yelled.With the crowd at the main stadium loudly supporting Jabeur at times, Gauff did not play badly in the opening set. But No. 8 seed Jabeur — a three-time major finalist — was superb, winning 17 of 18 first-serve points, never facing a single break point and accumulating a 12-5 edge in total winners.When she delivered an ace at 114 mph (184 kph) to end the set, Jabeur nodded repeatedly.“She’s a tough opponent and she’s well-loved on tour. I could tell by the crowd today — I know you guys wanted her to win. Honestly, whenever she’s not playing (me), I cheer for her, too,” Gauff said.“Even though you guys were for Ons, I really had a lot of fun, even when I lost the first set and they were chanting when I was in the bathroom," Gauff said about her trip off the court after the first set. "I was like, ‘This is just really fun, win or lose.’ It is.”Gauff got going after that, raising her level and trying to gain the upper hand during lengthier exchanges. She put in 16 winners over the last two sets, while breaking serve four times.“I know I have a lot of love here in Paris. Trust me, I know," said Gauff, who won the French Open junior title at age 14. "So I really appreciate it, and hopefully you guys can help me make it through the next round.”

The criminal charges against world No. 1 golfer Scottie Scheffler have been dismissed following his arrest earlier this month at the PGA Championship in Louisville, Kentucky."Based upon the totality of the evidence, my office cannot move forward in the prosecution of the charges filed against Mr. Scheffler," Jefferson County Attorney Mike O'Connell said at a brief hearing Wednesday. "Mr. Scheffler's actions and the evidence surrounding their exchange during the misunderstanding do not satisfy the elements of any criminal offenses," O'Connell added. The judge then accepted his motion to have the charges dismissed.Scheffler, 27, was taken into custody by Louisville Police on May 17 outside Valhalla Golf Club ahead of the second round of the tournament. He was booked on four criminal counts, including assault of a police officer, criminal mischief, reckless driving and disregarding signals from officers directing traffic.A police report obtained by Scripps News says he attempted to drive around traffic that was caused by a fatal accident near the country club. The report says Scheffler "refused to comply" with an officer directing traffic and "accelerated forward, dragging Detective Gillis to the ground."The officer was reportedly transported to a nearby hospital to be examined for "pain, swelling and abrasions to his left wrist and knee."Surveillance footage released by Louisville police last week appeared to show Gillis approaching Scheffler's vehicle on foot before stopping him from entering the golf course. Scheffler can later be seen being led away in handcuffs.In a statement released by the PGA Tour following his arrest, Scheffler described the incident as a "big misunderstanding.""I was proceeding as directed by police officers," he said. "It was a very chaotic situation, understandably so considering the tragic accident that had occurred earlier, and there was a big misunderstanding of what I thought I was being asked to do. I never intended to disregard any of the instructions."Louisville police said last week they were looking into whether officers violated any department policies during the arrest. Gillis has since been disciplined for not having his body camera activated at the time of the incident.

Health authorities in France are sounding the alarm as cases of dengue continue to rise ahead of the 2024 Olympic Games.Officials say that this year alone there have been about “1,649 imported cases,” compared to about 131 cases reported around the same time last year, according to Euronews.The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control says that the bulk of these cases stem from Guadeloupe and Martinique, where an "epidemic" is currently underway, as French Guiana has reported 7,000 confirmed dengue cases since the beginning of 2024.Officials are concerned because the Paris 2024 Olympic Games are only a few months away and scheduled to start on July 26, 2024.However, the French are not the only ones affected. This year, over 5 million cases have been reported worldwide that have resulted in 2,000 deaths, the ECDPC reports.The World Health Organization says that most of these cases are coming from the Americas, with Brazil, Argentina and Puerto Rico leading in cases.In March, Puerto Rico declared a public health emergency as the island reported 549 cases, nearly half of the total for the entire year of 2023 (1,242 cases). As of its latest data from April, the number had risen to 795.Dengue is a disease spread by mosquito bites, and symptoms include high fever, severe headache, muscle and joint pains, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands, rash, difficulty breathing, fatigue, and eye pain. If you have any of these symptoms, officials say to contact your primary care physician.

Palm Beach Gardens police have launched an investigation into professional golfer Grayson Murray's death. Police said Murray's body was found in a home at approximately 11 a.m. on May 25. Just one day prior, Murray had withdrawn from the Charles Schwab Challenge, citing an illness.Murray's parents confirmed to the PGA Tour that the 30-year-old "took his own life."The initial investigation did not reveal any signs of foul play, Palm Beach Gardens police said.Police added that no further information will be released during the investigation.The 30-year-old golfer won three consecutive Callaway Junior World Championships and became the top-ranked golfer in his age group. When Murray was 16, he made the first cut on the Korn Ferry Tour, and became the second-youngest player to achieve the victory.Murray would later go on to Wake Forest University, East Carolina University, and Arizona State University, before he got his break in 2016 gaining a sponsor’s exemption into the Korn Ferry Tour near Raleigh, North Carolina — his hometown — the PGA Tour said.Murray was able to earn full status on the PGA Tour for the 2016-2017 season.

Caitlin Clark, Angel Reese, Cameron Brink and others make this one of the most anticipated WNBA drafts in recent years. There are several impact players up for grabs, but their talent is nearly eclipsed by their popularity among basketball fans."Caitlin is kind of in a world of her own, but I don't know that we have seen this kind of excitement across the board," ESPN analyst Rebecca Lobo said. "You know, Angel Reese has a massive following. Cameron Brink has a large following of people, whether it's following them on social media or following them throughout the course of their college career."We have women coming into the draft this year, who people are very much aware of and eager to see how their game is going to translate at this level."Clark has helped bring millions of new fans to the game with her signature logo shots and dazzling passing ability. The Iowa star was a big reason why a record 18.9 million viewers tuned in to the NCAA championship game where South Carolina beat the Hawkeyes.The NCAA Division I all-time scoring leader will go first to the Indiana Fever on Monday night when the draft takes place at the Brooklyn Academy of Music in front of 1,000 fans."This is the first time we're going to have fans at the draft, so I think that's going to be special," ESPN analyst Andraya Carter said. "For people watching at home to see and hear a crowd and fans and people there, I think it'll be really exciting."While Clark is a lock to go first, Brink, Tennessee's Rickea Jackson and South Carolina's Kamilla Cardoso have all been in the discussion to be taken at No. 2 by Los Angeles. The Sparks also own the No. 4 pick with Chicago choosing third."They are foundational. They're an incredible opportunity for our organization," Sparks GM Raegan Pebley said. "We definitely want to see two players that not only have the skill set to make an impact early, but also a long runway ahead of them, opportunities to develop, opportunities to, not only be excellent in what they do, but how they impact the other pieces around them as we continue to build this team."Dallas is fifth and Washington sixth. Minnesota, Chicago, Dallas, Connecticut, New York and Atlanta close out the first round. In all, there are three rounds and 36 picks in total.SEE MORE: University of Iowa to retire Caitlin Clark's No. 22 jerseyAll-Americans Mackenzie Holmes of Indiana and Elizabeth Kitley of Virginia Tech won't be able to play in the WNBA this season because of knee injuries. Holmes said on social media that she is having surgery next month."At this time to ensure my body is healthy and my playing career is as long and successful as possible, I have decided to get the necessary surgery in May to prevent further issues and alleviate the pain it has caused," she said. If you've ever admired a perfectly golden Thanksgiving turkey and wondered how professional chefs make it look so good, Okeechobee Steakhouse co-owner Ralph Lewis has a surprisingly simple answer."It's butter."And not just a little butter.During a recent Thanksgiving cooking demonstration at Okeechobee Prime Meat Market, Lewis stood beside a giant inflatable stick of butter, worked from a table piled high with butter and seasonings, and even pulled a backup rubber stick of butter from his pocket.For Lewis, butter isn't simply an ingredient. It's the foundation of a great Thanksgiving turkey."Are you really supposed to have a budget with butter?" Lewis joked. "Those two words do not go together."According to Lewis, the biggest mistake many home cooks make is putting all of their butter on the outside of the bird.Instead, he recommends carefully separating the skin from the breast meat and creating pockets beneath the skin.Once those pockets are created, it's time to start adding butter.Lots of butter."You just want to keep working it in there," Lewis said. That's impossible, literally impossible, and that's a chef's code."As the turkey cooks, the butter melts beneath the skin, helping keep the meat moist while contributing to the rich color and flavor many Thanksgiving hosts are trying to achieve.After working butter beneath the skin, Lewis also coats the outside of the turkey before adding seasoning.One of the most useful tips Lewis shared involves seasoning the butter before it ever touches the bird.Start by taking butter out of the refrigerator and allowing it to soften to room temperature.Then combine the softened butter with herbs and seasonings such as:Kosher saltFreshly ground black pepperThymeRosemarySageMix everything together until it forms a seasoned compound butter.Then spread that butter beneath the skin and across the exterior of the turkey.By combining the herbs and seasoning directly into the butter, the flavors are distributed more evenly throughout the turkey as it cooks.Lewis says it's a simple step that can make a noticeable difference in flavor.Allow butter to come to room temperature.Mix the butter with kosher salt, black pepper, thyme, rosemary, sage or your favorite herbs.Gently separate the skin from the breast meat without tearing it.Spread seasoned butter beneath the skin and continue working it throughout the breast area.Coat the exterior of the turkey with additional butter.Add additional herbs and seasoning as desired.Place about a half-inch to one inch of water, chicken stock or turkey stock in the bottom of the pan.Cover the turkey with foil and roast at approximately 325 degrees.About 30 minutes before the turkey is done, remove the foil and increase the heat.Lewis says this final step helps create the deep golden-brown color that makes a Thanksgiving turkey look picture-perfect.Of course, Lewis' demonstration included a healthy helping of humor.At one point, while explaining his butter-heavy technique, he declared there is no such thing as too much butter.When told that Thanksgiving calories don't count, he quickly fired back:"What's calories?"And when asked whether anything should go inside the turkey cavity itself, his answer was immediate."Well, butter, of course."For families looking to spend less time in the kitchen and more time around the dinner table, Okeechobee Prime Meat Market is offering a variety of Thanksgiving meal packages featuring roasted or smoked turkeys, prime rib, beef tenderloin, traditional sides and holiday desserts.The market's Ultimate Holiday Family Feast serves 16 to 18 people and includes a Bell & Evans all-natural turkey, prime roasted beef tenderloin, stuffing, mashed potatoes, gravy, cranberry sauce and more.Pre-orders are available through Okeechobee Prime Meat Market in West Palm Beach.This article was drafted with the assistance of Microsoft Copilot using reporting, interview transcripts, and information gathered by WPTV journalist T.A. An anonymous donation expected to exceed $50 million is helping cover tuition costs for medical laboratory science students at the University of Washington for the next half-century.The dean of the university's School of Medicine, Dr. Tim Dellit, made the surprise announcement Monday to about 30 grateful undergrads, who will each see two quarters' worth of tuition covered for their senior-year clinical rotations, The Seattle Times reported."I'm really shocked," said Jasmine Wertz, eyes filling with tears. Extremely grateful."Students in the program are trained to perform clinical lab tests on patient samples, which are used to help diagnose, treat and prevent disease and other conditions. Their clinical rotations are so time-consuming that it's hard to hold down part-time jobs during them.RELATED STORY | Trump Administration details plans to further dismantle Department of EducationThe gift is the latest in a series of recent donations helping pay for college around the country. Last year, the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York received a $1 billion donation from Ruth Gottesman, a former professor and the widow of a Wall Street investor, making tuition there free.Most medical students at Johns Hopkins University no longer pay tuition thanks to a $1 billion gift from Bloomberg Philanthropies.In September at Marshall University in West Virginia, President Brad Smith and his wife, Alys Smith, announced a $50 million gift to promote a program aimed at eliminating student debt, in part by covering tuition for West Virginia students with family income of $65,000 or less.The University of Washington announcement on Monday is worth about $8,000 to $10,000 per student, said UW Medicine spokesperson Susan Gregg. The program will also be able to expand from 70 to 100 students over the next 10 years.The donor, from Washington state, wishes to remain anonymous, but "had a relationship with this program," Gregg said. The donor is also a fan of the local burger chain Dick's, and burgers were piled high atop platters as the students celebrated.ICYMI | Brown University rejects Trump administration's higher education proposalThe field of medical laboratory services has faced increasing demand and an aging workforce in Washington, according to UW Medicine. Those factors have resulted in an "urgent need to grow the pipeline of highly skilled clinical laboratory professionals," the health care system said in a news release."You are the glue, in many ways, of our entire health system," Dellit told the students. "You are the unsung heroes. You work behind the scenes that allow all of the health care machinery to work."

Body camera video captured the moments on Sunday morning when a Riviera Beach officer helped a family of four escape their home after their truck caught fire.Officer Andrew Hinds spoke with WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache about how it all happened.WATCH BELOW: Officers alert family after truck fire threatens homeHinds called it a case of being at the right place, at the right time."Honestly, I'm just relieved that everybody got out and it didn’t spread anymore," said Hinds.Hinds was on regular patrol duty at about 10 a.m. when he noticed smoke."While we were doing traffic, we looked up and saw smoke coming from a house," said Hinds.Officers rushed towards the house and found a truck engulfed in flames."Residents were flagging us down, telling us there were people inside; some small kids and a family," said Hinds.Hinds was the one to call dispatch and notify them of the truck fire. Officers rushed to the door and began knocking before the fire spread."Your house, look! It's going to be set on fire! Anybody else in the house? Hurry up, get out," Hinds could be heard telling the family inside the home. "Go go go go go!"Hinds said the family of four was asleep and unaware of the flames. His priority was to rush them to safety."Honestly, you could hear the crackling from the car going on fire," said Hinds. "In my mind, I'm like, OK, they probably have gas in there. I don't know how long I have to hurry everybody out. "So it was nice that we just happened to be at the right time at the right place."

King tides are the highest tides of the year, and they are increasingly flooding coastal communities as sea levels rise.King tide is a non-scientific or colloquial term that people often use to describe these exceptionally high tides. The 2026 super El Niño — the natural and temporary warming of parts of the Pacific — has raised coastal water levels and intensified the effects of king tides."Tides are incredibly complicated. Really every location has different tidal cycles and that's the basis for what a king tide is," said Alec Bogdanoff, an oceanographer and meteorologist in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. "It's a local term for the highest high tides of the year in a location. And when it impacts you, that's when they call it a king tide."King tides are happening more oftenKing tides typically occur when the sun, moon and Earth are nearly aligned because their gravitational pull adds together. This raises water levels and produces the greatest tidal effects of the year. This can happen on both coasts around the same time because the tides are responding to the same alignment and proximity of the moon and sun. In 2026, El Niño caused higher baseline water levels on both coasts, Bogdanoff said.The highest high tides happen during full moons and new moons and seasonal cycles that can raise or lower sea levels, he added.Historically, many coastal areas saw king tides once or twice a year, but some places are experiencing them more often than that as sea levels rise.King tides can cause floods in coastal communitiesBecause king tides bring unusually high water levels, they can cause local tidal flooding. Strong winds and storms can make that flooding worse.Bogdanoff said the stormwater systems don't function normally when ocean water is higher than the levels they were designed for.Climate change is raising risksClimate change is driving and accelerating sea level rise. Glaciers and ice sheets are melting and the sea's waters are expanding as they warm. As this happens, flooding from king tides is becoming more frequent and it's increasingly disrupting life along the coasts.Four California locations recorded their all-time highest observed water levels in late October, and near-record king tides flooded some low-lying communities there as Thanksgiving travel ramped up."El Niño is natural, the sea level rise we're seeing now isn't," Bogdanoff said. "The flooding we're seeing with these king tides is a preview of what's to come in the 2030s and beyond."In 2011, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency said sea level rise will make current king tides become the future's everyday tides.Coastal areas prepare for king tidesBogdanoff said coastal communities can do stormwater assessments and adaptation plans that take into account future projections for sea level rise, like his home state is doing with its Resilient Florida Program. Bogdanoff is principal scientist and co-founder of Brizaga, an engineering and consulting firm that helps communities plan for flooding and sea level rise.Next steps could include raising roads, figuring out better ways to protect the coastlines, finding more green space that absorbs water and building bigger stormwater systems that rely more on pumps than gravity to drain the water quicker — projects that will take time, he added."In some communities it's a much bigger conversation about what the future looks like," he said. "We don't have to fix everything at once. We just need to make sure the next decision is a little smarter than the last one."

An 18-year-old was killed and six others were wounded in a Thanksgiving morning shooting at a Polk County Airbnb where investigators say dozens of young people had gathered for a party advertised on social media.Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said deputies responded to the shooting on Captiva Drive shortly before 1 a.m. Thursday. Investigators believe more than 50 people were at the rental property when gunfire erupted, with many of those attending being juveniles.WATCH BELOW: Polk County Airbnb shooting leaves 1 dead, 6 others woundedThe person killed was identified by Judd as 18-year-old Oral Walker Jr. of Orlando. He was shot multiple times and died at the scene, according to the sheriff.Six other people were shot, including teenagers ages 15, 16 and 17, as well as an 18-year-old and a 21-year-old. A 15-year-old girl who was shot in the chest was initially listed in critical condition and placed on a ventilator, Judd said. Investigators were later told she had stabilized and was expected to survive.The other victims suffered what Judd described as less serious gunshot wounds, including wounds to their arms and legs.According to Judd, the gathering was promoted on social media as a birthday pajama party for a juvenile. Judd said preliminary information indicates a 16-year-old girl was involved in organizing the gathering but could not have rented the property herself. Witnesses told investigators that an adult, possibly her brother or another young adult, rented it.Judd stressed that those details could change as detectives continue conducting interviews and gathering evidence.Investigators believe multiple guns were involved and said at least one firearm had been recovered.Judd said a witness told detectives that Walker pulled a gun and began firing during the party. An unidentified person then allegedly pulled another gun and shot Walker multiple times.The sheriff cautioned that the account was based on information gathered early in the investigation and had not yet been fully corroborated.Judd said investigators want to identify and speak with the person who shot Walker. Based on the initial witness account, he said detectives are examining whether that person may have acted in self-defense."We need to talk to you," Judd said, urging the person to come forward.Judd also said Walker had an extensive history of criminal charges, primarily in Orange County, and was on juvenile probation. Those claims were made by the sheriff during Thursday's news conference as he criticized how previous cases involving Walker had been handled.Five people had been arrested as of Thursday morning in connection with circumstances surrounding the investigation, although Judd said the group included both adults and juveniles and did not immediately detail all of the charges.Among those arrested was the mother of the juvenile whose birthday was allegedly being celebrated. Judd said Brianna Jacques, 45, was taken into custody after arriving at the scene and allegedly creating a disturbance and resisting deputies as investigators spoke with her daughter. Jacques faces charges of breach of peace, resisting arrest without violence and contributing to the delinquency of a minor.The sheriff repeatedly appealed to the dozens of people who were at the party to cooperate with detectives, saying many fled after the gunfire began."We need your help," Judd said.Detectives were continuing to interview witnesses, process the scene and track down people who attended the party Thursday morning. Judd said investigators also planned to examine the circumstances surrounding the rental of the property.

The 19-year-old son of a Florida county commissioner was shot and killed while camping in Santa Rosa County on Sunday.Carey Washington Vinson, a history major at Florida State University, was the son of Joe Vinson, who was recently elected to the Escambia County Commission.The Santa Rosa County Sheriff's Office said investigators are working to identify those involved in Carey's death and determine the circumstances surrounding the shooting. "It was not a 'stray bullet' that killed our Wash."According to Vinson, the family understands that someone stood on the opposite bank of the river and pointed a gun toward the occupied sandbar campground.He said the shooters were close enough to see the campfire and hear people talking."They fired shot after shot with malicious intent," Vinson wrote, alleging that the shooters fired another round after campers screamed for them to stop, then laughed as they drove away.Those details reflect the family's understanding of the shooting. The sheriff's office has not publicly confirmed that account in the statement provided.Vinson remembered his son as a thoughtful, outgoing young man who loved history, music and adventure. A FedEx airplane overran a runway at the Miami International Airport on Wednesday night, forcing all but one runway to temporarily close the day before Thanksgiving, according to officials.There were no reports of injuries after the plane ran off the runway at about 8:40 p.m., the airport reported. The incident happened almost three months after an Amazon cargo jet overshot another runway in Miami, killing five people on the ground.By early Thursday, the Federal Aviation Administration was reporting hourslong flight delays.The FAA, which is investigating, said the McDonnell Douglas MD-11 was coming from Memphis.FedEx said the plane had "an issue upon landing" and that it is coordinating with investigating officials."We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries," the company said in a statement.FedEx had just started flying MD-11s again in May to deliver packages after that type of plane crashed in Kentucky last year as it was taking off. The UPS plane's left engine flew off and three pilots along with 12 people on the ground were killed. The FAA had approved Boeing’s proposed fix for the MD-11s “after extensive review.”The airport recommended that passengers scheduled to fly Wednesday night should check with their airlines for the latest flight updates before traveling to the airport.“We appreciate our passengers’ patience as we work to safely resume normal operations,” the airport said in a statement.The runway this FedEx plane landed on Wednesday is different than the one the Amazon cargo plane overran in September. But three of Miami’s runways converge at the west end, so the FedEx plane ended up close to where the Amazon plane careened across a road and struck a van filled with a plane cleaning crew.The incident also comes less than two weeks after a minor collision between two planes at a taxiway intersection at the Miami airport. The wing of the Copa flight and the nose of the UPS plane collided.Miami-Dade Fire Rescue units responded to the incident Wednesday. The National Transportation Safety Board said it had no information about the situation.

What is the best golf course in America?Golf.com broke down the top 100 courses, which they call a "Top 100 Courses in the U.S. for 2026-27: The ultimate bucket list for American golf".So, how do they determine the list? It's a democratic vote with the panelists.Golf.com said each panelist gets a ballot with hundreds of courses. Beside the list of courses are 11 groupings. If a panelist considers a course to be among the top three in the U.S., they tick the first column. If they believe the course to be among Nos. 4-10, they check that column, followed by 11-25 and so on. They even have a column for “remove.” The organization is also careful with panelist selections to include a variety of input and to avoid anyone with ties to any of the courses.Research shows golf is experiencing a resurgence as a hobby. The National Golf Foundation reports that 30.6 million Americans play golf, that's up 1.7 million from the previous year and a new record.Did any Florida courses make the list?Course: TPC Sawgrass (Players Stadium), Ponte Vedra BeachRank: 53Built: 1981Designer: Pete DyeCourse: Seminole, Juno BeachRank: 17Built: 1926Designer: Donald Ross

More than 140 passengers and crew on board a cruise ship that departed from South Florida last week have reported becoming sick with a mystery gastrointestinal illness, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says.According to information provided by the CDC, the Princess Cruises ship Caribbean Princess departed Port Everglades in Fort Lauderdale on Nov. 11 on a 12-night journey. The outbreak was then reported days later on Nov. 15.RELATED STORY | Nearly 200 passengers rescued after tanker hits river boat in New Orleans: 'Miracle on the Mississippi'At least 134 of 2,936 passengers and 14 of the 1,132 crew members have reported symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea, according to the CDC.In response to the outbreak, Princess Cruises and the crew on board the ship said there have been increased cleaning and disinfection efforts according to their outbreak and response plan.In addition, passengers and crew who are sick have been isolated."Norovirus is often the cause of gastrointestinal illness outbreaks on cruise ships, but we don't always know the cause of the outbreak when we begin an investigation," the CDC said on its website. "Finding the agent that caused an outbreak (causative agent) can take time."So far, the cause of the illness is unknown."Princess Cruises can confirm that a limited number of guests aboard Caribbean Princess have reported mild gastrointestinal illness," the cruise line said in a statement to CBS News Miami. "Our crew responded promptly by implementing enhanced sanitation protocols across the ship, including comprehensive cleaning and disinfection measures."RELATED STORY | CDC sidelines itself as hantavirus cruise ship outbreak grabs global attentionThe statement says that while most guests remain unaffected by the illness, it is continuing to monitor the situation.According to the CDC, cases of illnesses that have been reported are totals for the entire voyage."It does not mean all people are sick at the same time, such as when they arrive or leave a port or ship," the CDC continued.The Caribbean Princess departed Fort Lauderdale on a round-trip, 12-day Panama Canal trip that is expected to return on Nov. 23.
