Gov. Ron DeSantis said Florida is preparing to seek additional federal disaster assistance after a second round of historic flooding inundated communities across the state, with the St. Johns River reaching record levels and hundreds of people requiring rescue.Speaking Monday in Brevard County alongside state and local emergency officials, DeSantis said parts of Cocoa Beach and surrounding communities received 15 to 20 inches of rain in recent days. Many of those areas were still recovering from severe flooding earlier this month.WATCH BELOW: Florida seeking more federal aid after historic flooding, according to DeSantisDeSantis said the St. Johns River near Cocoa reached nearly 19 feet on Saturday, surpassing the previous record by more than a foot. He warned that because the river moves slowly, flooding could take weeks or even months to fully recede."There could be more flooding that happens in the near future," DeSantis said. "The St. Johns River is a major concern just given how high it has gotten."Florida previously requested a major federal disaster declaration following the first round of flooding earlier this month. DeSantis said that request is awaiting action from the federal government.The state is now collecting damage assessments from the latest flooding and plans to submit another request for a major disaster declaration. DeSantis said the second request will cover a broader area because more counties and communities were affected by the latest rainfall.Florida Division of Emergency Management Executive Director Jared Perdue said the state could have enough damage information to move forward with the request as soon as Monday or Tuesday.DeSantis said he expects the request to warrant federal approval."It's basically just the damage assessments trying to show that there's been enough damage to justify federal intervention," DeSantis said. "And I think in this case that that has been the case."DeSantis also said individual assistance included in the state's initial request could provide some relief to residents with damaged homes, including those who did not carry flood insurance. However, he cautioned that federal assistance may not cover the full amount of a homeowner's losses.State agencies, including the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, Florida National Guard, Florida State Guard and Florida Highway Patrol, have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues, according to DeSantis.The Florida National Guard has mobilized 421 personnel and conducted 417 welfare checks, while deploying 54 high-water vehicles across six counties.Another 173 FWC officers are deployed, along with more than 200 FHP troopers assisting flooded communities, stranded motorists and disabled vehicles.Nearly 160 Florida State Guard personnel have also been mobilized. State Guard crews have helped with "muck and gut" operations at more than 250 properties in Brevard and Okeechobee counties, removing water-damaged material from flooded homes.The state has distributed more than 22,000 boxes of water, 7,500 ready-to-eat meals, 1,200 flood cleanup buckets and 1,300 tarps to affected communities, according to Perdue.Emergency officials warned that high water remains a threat even as conditions begin to improve.Perdue said State Road 50 in Brevard County and State Road 46 in Seminole County remained underwater as of Monday."If there are any state roads or local roads that are underwater, please do not drive or walk through the water," Perdue said. "It can be very dangerous. You just can't see what's down there."The Florida Division of Emergency Management has deployed more than 10,000 feet of temporary flood barriers to protect critical infrastructure, including government buildings and lift stations in Seminole County and HCA Florida Lake Monroe Hospital in Sanford.The state has also deployed 90 pumps and 22 vacuum trucks during the response in Brevard, Broward, Indian River, Flagler, Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Volusia counties.FDOT has more than 750 personnel working on flood assessments and pumping operations across Central and South Florida, DeSantis said.A shelter remains open at the Joseph N. Davis Community Center in Melbourne.Four multi-agency resource centers have also been established across three counties, including two in Brevard County. DeSantis said more than 1,600 residents have already received assistance through the centers. The centers will be closed on Thanksgiving.Residents whose homes are uninhabitable because of flooding can also apply for the state's temporary travel trailer program through emergencyRV.org.DeSantis said state resources will remain in affected communities throughout the recovery."Our folks aren't going anywhere," DeSantis said. We're going to see through the federal assistance and make sure that people can get back on their feet."

The 37th Stuart Air Show brought aviation fans young and old together for a picture-perfect weekend filled with aircraft, family traditions, and appreciation for veterans.Organizers said the weekend got off to a strong start Friday night with a drone and fireworks show and continued with large crowds throughout the weekend."Stuart Air Show has had an amazing weekend Friday night with our drone and fireworks show. We had a great turnout," Chrissy Valvano said. "Sunday, we're looking at a record turnout for Veterans Appreciation Day, and this weather could not be better."For some families, attending the Stuart Air Show has become a tradition passed down through the years."The Stuart Air Show has been a part of our community for many years," Sarah Naylor said. "We have many memories of coming in the past, as long as I can remember."For younger aviation fans Wyatt and Ivy Rotan, some of the biggest attractions were the military aircraft."I like coming to the Stuart Air Show because I like to see the C-17 and the F-16 fly," Wyatt said."I like seeing the C-17," Ivy added.The event also gave young people a chance to learn more about aviation while honoring those who served."You get to have a lot of fun around here, just going around and seeing a bunch of planes," John Gefell said. "Also, because I'm working on my aviation merit badge as a Boy Scout and my grandpa was a veteran, so it’s just real fun to come out here and just have a lot of fun."With beautiful weather and a strong turnout, the 37th Stuart Air Show once again brought the community together, giving longtime fans and a new generation of aviation enthusiasts a weekend to remember.

The Stuart Air Show is preparing to take flight at Witham Field, bringing aircraft, crowds and heavier traffic to the Stuart area.WATCH WPTV'S REPORT:The air show is celebrating its 37th year at Witham Field on Friday and this year's event will feature the F-16 demo team along with a variety of other aircraft. The show runs through Sunday, Nov. 15.WATCH BELOW: What to know about traffic, parking and getting to Witham FieldAmong those participating is Maj. Taylor Hiester, the United States Air Force F-16 Viper Demonstration Team Commander and Pilot stationed at Shaw Air Force Base in Sumter, South Carolina."I've been in the Air Force for 11 years now, and it's been a dream come true for the last three years to serve, not just as a military officer first, but fighter pilot second," Hiester told WPTV Anchor Mike Trim. "To be the American fighter pilot that gets to connect the American people with the people that do their business around the world on their behalf, is very special."The 37th annual air show features F-16s, large military planes, ghost riders, aerobatic planes and skydivers, along with games and food for families."It's for me, my last performance and for a lot of performers, it's that it's the close out of the year," Hiester told WPTV. "So, it is a wonderful cocktail of emotions that come together that make a fantastic show for the people of Florida, and I think that the people are going to notice that there's something special."Beyond the flight demonstrations, the event also focused on education and STEM classesWPTV First Alert Weather Meteorologist Kate Wentzel spoke with students from the aerospace club from Jupiter Christian, along with students from the Parker area, the Virginia Beach area, Fort Pierce and around the Treasure Coast. "In the air show, they want to partner with all of these school groups and organizations, because really it empowers them and inspires them to go into aviation-related careers," Wentzel said.Weather plays a critical role in aviation, and the students learned how it affects pilots."We talked about winds, how that impacts pilots. Pilots want to take off into the wind, because the wind blowing over the wings, gives them better lift and a faster lift speed," Wentzel said. "They also want to land into the wind, because if they have a tailwind pushing them too strong, it can make it difficult for the pilot to have a controlled landing."Students also learned how icing can impact aircraft at high altitudes and near thunderstorms. Aircraft are supposed to stay 20 miles away from severe thunderstorms at all times, because that is where big updrafts and gusty winds develop, Wentzel said.Conditions are expected to be clear and breezy this evening, making for good viewing of the Stuart Air Show.

Just weeks after historic flooding destroyed homes and displaced families in Jensen Beach, Martin County residents are bracing for another round of heavy rain — with up to 12 inches forecast over the next three days.For families still struggling to recover, the threat of more flooding comes as county commissioners work to determine what caused the initial disaster and how to help those who lost nearly everything.On Tuesday, flood victims packed a Martin County Commission meeting, pleading for financial assistance and answers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Along Cheri Drive in Jensen Beach, the signs of destruction remain. Dumpsters line driveways, damaged belongings sit outside and families are still trying to salvage what's left of their homes.Lisa French, her husband, Jeremy, and their two young sons are among those displaced after floodwaters rose as high as 3 feet inside some homes two weeks ago."It's like we're kind of stuck," French told WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey. French said her home had about 3 to 6 inches of flooding that sat inside for more than a week, causing mold to grow 3 to 4 feet up the walls. "So they, yeah, they tore the walls down in the house," said French. "They just chipped up the last bit of the tile, and it's empty." Now, with more rain approaching, French fears her family could face another disaster before recovering from the first."Of course, we're afraid because we all flooded in our houses," she said.New figures released by Martin County show at least 36 homes sustained damage, with an estimated $3 million in residential losses. Commissioners estimated another $14 million in damage to beaches, and at least $1 million in damage to roadways that now need repairs. For some residents, the destruction represents a lifetime of memories washed away."We've lost everything," one elderly Jensen Beach resident told commissioners. "We have 60 years of our life — kids, grandkids, everything. It's all gone."As residents demand answers about what went wrong, commissioners approved shifting $200,000 from the county's stormwater budget to investigate whether development and changes to local drainage systems contributed to the flooding.Commissioner Blake Capps called the investigation "a good starting point.""It may be that we need to augment the study beyond the $200,000 that we approve today," said Capps. Meanwhile, county crews are working around the clock to prepare for the next storm, lowering retention pond levels, deploying additional pumps and draining flooded properties."We have people 24 hours a day pumping that material down," Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton said.Commissioners also approved financial assistance for eligible flood victims through the state's State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program.The assistance includes grants of up to $25,000 for income-eligible homeowners and loans of up to $75,000 secured by liens on their properties.But there's a catch: The grants are reimbursement-based, meaning homeowners must first pay for eligible repairs before receiving the money.For families who lost everything, that presents another obstacle."We don't have $25,000," French said. "A lot of people don't have $25,000, so it's great, and we're appreciative, but I mean, our house is empty, and $25,000 is not going to do much for us." The other problem: the county currently has just $1 million in SHIP funding available, and commissioners warned the money could run out quickly, even with additional state funding promised."They haven't given us the amount yet, but they have assured us that we will be getting some disaster relief funds," said Human Services Director Michelle Miller Strict income limits could also disqualify some flood victims who cannot afford to rebuild on their own. The income cap for a family of one is $86,040. The cap for a family of two is $98,400. For a family of four, it's $122,880. When reporter Kate Hussey asked Capps what would happen to those families, he acknowledged the county needs to explore other options."There are going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where someone barely missed the limit, and we're going to need to take a look at what we can do for those folks," Capps said.For residents like French, the need is immediate."We just need somebody to step up," she said. "We need funding." With another round of heavy rain approaching, Martin County is distributing sandbags at Halpatiokee Regional Park to help residents protect their properties, with a limit of 25 per person. The County's Emergency Operations Center is scheduled to be staffed beginning Tuesday at 2 p.m., and the county is coordinating with the National Weather Service and Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM).Fire Rescue is also standing by with multiple high-water rescue trucks.Commissioners also said a Federal Emergency Management Agency representative is expected to visit Nov. 30 to assess the damage — a potential step toward securing federal disaster assistance.But for families still displaced and facing the possibility of more flooding, the uncertainty remains.

Weeks after historic flooding devastated homes in Jensen Beach, Martin County families are still cleaning up and rebuilding, with volunteers, churches, firefighters, contractors and local leaders joining the recovery effort.Water marks remain visible on some homes, showing how high floodwaters rose. Residents are now removing damaged drywall, clearing debris and collecting donated supplies while seeking financial assistance and answers about the area's drainage systems.Neighbors step in to help Jensen Beach familiesBefore-and-after video from the Jensen Beach neighborhood shows the extent of the flooding, which left several homes under feet of water.Weeks later, homeowner Lisa Marie French said cleaning up has been a major undertaking. We first told you about French's circumstances last week. You first have to empty the houses," French said. "We have to clean the houses; they're filled with mold, we have to take the drywall out."French, whose home was impacted by the flooding, has also helped coordinate community cleanup efforts alongside Christ of Church, Family Church and other organizations. She said neighbors and other volunteers have repeatedly shown up asking what families need and then immediately gotten to work."People have been just coming and just hands-on," French said. "People are like, 'Hey, are you taking donations? What do you need?' And they get out of their cars, and they start working, and that's our neighbors. It’s pretty amazing."Residents seek answers about flooding and drainageAs cleanup continues, residents say they also want answers about what contributed to the severe flooding.Some are questioning how much pumping from Port St. Lucie and Fort Pierce into the Savannas Preserve may have contributed to flooding in their neighborhood.Stephen Leighton, chief of staff for U.S. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla., told WPTV that questions remain as officials work through the recovery process."There's a lot of answers that these residents need, and hopefully we can do that," Leighton said.Leighton also said the state had taken steps toward an emergency declaration and reached out to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA).Families look for financial assistanceFor some homeowners, rebuilding also brings financial uncertainty.French said her home is not in a flood zone and she does not have flood insurance, leaving her family dependent on whatever assistance, donated materials and volunteer help becomes available."We're trying to get any type of help. We don't have flood insurance here," French said. "We're way above sea level; we are not a flood zone. So it's just whatever volunteers and help and materials we can get is what we get."Community calls for more volunteersResidents say more hands are still needed as families work to make their homes livable again.Leighton said a question-and-answer town meeting with residents and county, state and federal officials is planned this week as the community seeks clarity about the flooding and available assistance.For volunteers, Leighton said even small acts can make a difference for families trying to put their lives back together."To help somebody take that picture off the wall and put it in a box, so they can move on, is a big deal," he said.With Thanksgiving approaching, he said the need for community support remains urgent."We're two weeks out from Thanksgiving, and we really need the community to come together and help," Leighton said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. What was once a sprawling cattle pasture in western Martin County now looks more like a lake.What residents described as 3 to 4 feet of floodwater currently covers parts of Hungryland Farms in the Trailside community, forcing cattle to wade and swim through submerged pastures in search of dry ground.WATCH REPORT BELOW: But for the families who live and work there, the flooding is more than a natural disaster. They say it's a crisis years in the making — one they warned officials about as far back as 2018.Documents obtained by WPTV show residents raised concerns about drainage problems long before last week's historic rainfall inundated the Treasure Coast.Now, with the rain gone but the water lingering, residents are questioning whether the devastation could have been prevented.Melissa, who raises grass-fed cattle at Hungryland Farms in the rural Trailside community, says the flooding has transformed her property almost overnight."It feels like Lake Okeechobee," she said.Her cattle, accustomed to grazing freely across the farm, are now navigating deep floodwater. "It's completely covered," Melissa said. "All of our pastures ... they're all underwater."The flooding has left her animals without their primary food source and exposed them to potentially deadly hazards, including drowning, waterborne parasites and electrical dangers.Melissa pointed to an electrical transformer nearly submerged by floodwater, questioning whether her cattle could be electrocuted if they wandered too close.And despite the rain stopping, she said the water isn't draining — it's rising. "We always thought we were through because the rain had stopped, but the water kept rising," she said.For Trailside Homeowners Association President Kyla Shay, the flooding is the culmination of years of unresolved drainage concerns.In a 2018 letter obtained by WPTV, Shay warned homeowners that property south of Trailside had effectively become a reservoir, with water rising as much as 3.5 feet above community roads and breaching a berm — a raised barrier designed to control water flow.That same year, Shay contacted the South Florida Water Management District, warning that blocked drainage had left some pastures under 8 feet of water.She asked for help but says the underlying problems were never resolved."It's a combination of years of 'We'll get to it,' and we never got to it," Shay said.Martin County Public Works Director Jim Gorton acknowledges the community faces significant drainage challenges.Gorton said a berm breached Monday on the county-owned Elise J Property northeast of Trailside, sending water into a nearby canal, with some water backflowing into the community."We still can't get back to that breach," Gorton told investigative reporter Kate Hussey, explaining that high water levels have prevented crews from accessing the area.But the larger problem, he said, is Trailside's geography.The community is essentially a bathtub, surrounded by berms, hundreds of acres of wetlands and two independent water control districts.Water flows into the area, but there is only one drainage ditch for it to slowly escape."There's no easy way to get that water out except by pump or gravity," Gorton said.WPTV contacted engineer Bob Higgins, who works with both the Pal Mar Water Control District and the Hobe St. Lucie Conservancy District.Higgins said a potential solution had already been designed years ago: an outfall that would allow water to drain through the R G Mitigation Bank Preserve to the south and the neighboring Elise J property, which Martin County acquired in 2026. But that project was never built.When Hussey asked Gorton whether the county had been aware of the proposal, he confirmed officials had discussed it with the property's former owner."We did have some dialogue with the previous owner of Elise J about creating a formal water control structure that could discharge before the berms would breach," Gorton said.According to Gorton, the former owners submitted two permit applications to the South Florida Water Management District, but construction never began.WPTV contacted the former property owners, who said they did not know why the project was never completed.When Hussey reached out to the South Florida Water Management District, the agency said Trailside was outside its jurisdiction.However, Gorton said the district had permitted every property within Trailside and oversaw the proposed drainage project.Hussey followed up with the district, seeking clarification about its jurisdiction and asking why the drainage project was never constructed.The district has not responded to those follow-up questions.Despite the years of delays, Gorton said there may finally be a path forward."The good news is the county purchased that property, and it's our intent to bring that project forward," he said.Gorton said he has already requested the original permit applications in hopes of expediting approval — and construction— of the project.He also plans to return Friday to assess the flooding and determine what immediate relief may be possible."We're looking at ways to get the water out faster," he said.But for residents like Melissa, every additional day underwater carries a cost. "This could be a very costly natural disaster for us," she said.Her cattle still need to eat. Their pastures are submerged. And with no clear timeline for when the water will recede, the future of her farm remains uncertain."I don't have any food," Melissa said to her cows. "I'm sorry."For now, Hungryland Farms is living up to its name — and the families who depend on it are waiting for the water to go down.WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey continues to seek answers from the South Florida Water Management District about the proposed drainage project and why it was never completed.

St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, because additional heavy rainfall is expected overnight and into the morning, district officials announced Thursday.ADDITIONAL CLOSURES: Indian River County schools closed Friday due to flooding, heavy rain Palm Beach County schools to close Friday amid heavy rain, flood watchesThe district said it made the decision out of an abundance of caution because heavy rain could coincide with the morning arrival period while areas throughout the county are already saturated.After a break from the rain Thursday afternoon, the district said the National Weather Service is forecasting an additional 3 to 4 inches or more of rainfall, with the heaviest rain expected around the time students and staff would normally be traveling to school.“The safety of our students and staff is at the forefront of this decision,” Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince said. “Given the potential for heavy rainfall during the morning arrival period and the already saturated conditions throughout our community, we believe closing schools is the safest decision for our students, families, and employees.”All after-school programs scheduled for Friday are canceled, including aftercare, activities and athletic events, according to the district.The closure means students will begin their Thanksgiving holiday early. Students are scheduled to return to school Monday, Nov. 30.The district has not yet determined whether the SAT scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 21, will take place.Officials said a decision on the SAT will be made later Friday and communicated to families as soon as possible.This story has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Water service has been fully restored to the Tradition and western Port St. Lucie areas following a major water main break Tuesday, but a precautionary boil water notice remains in effect.The break happened near Glades Cut Off Road when a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged a 36-inch water main, according to city officials.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Crews completed repairs Tuesday evening and began flushing the water main shortly afterward.The city initially recommended a 48-hour precautionary boil water notice Tuesday at noon for the Tradition area, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, west of Interstate 95 to Becker Road.The notice also covers communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano.City officials said water quality testing began Wednesday. Because of the number of customers affected, a significant number of samples must be collected and tested before the notice can be lifted.Residents should continue boiling water until the city confirms it is safe to use without boiling. Restored water service does not mean the boil water notice has ended.The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible.Updates will be posted at CityofPSL.com.

About 21,000 customers in Port St. Lucie remain under a precautionary boil water notice after a contractor damaged a water main earlier this week.The city announced it is extending the notice for the Tradition and west Port St. Lucie areas following Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road.The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected.City officials said the notice will remain in place until water quality testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift.With an estimated 21,000 customers affected, officials said a significant number of water samples must be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe.The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water, warning that interference could delay testing and extend the notice.According to officials, the break was caused by a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city. Crews responded and repaired the damaged 36-inch water main within hours before beginning the required flushing process.The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible.There is no estimated time for when the boil water notice will be lifted.Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com.

A 24-year-old woman has died from injuries she suffered after she was struck while riding an electric scooter in a hit-and-run crash in Port St. Lucie, police said Wednesday.The woman died at approximately 9:23 p.m. Tuesday, according to the Port St. Lucie Police Department.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The crash happened around 5:10 a.m. Monday near the intersection of Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the woman was riding an electric scooter when a vehicle struck her. Investigators allege the driver left the scene without stopping to help her or notify law enforcement.The department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit later identified the vehicle as a gray Chevrolet Tahoe and located it at a Port St. Lucie home, according to police.Investigators identified the alleged driver as 18-year-old Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer.Police said investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing "ding dong ditch" with friends shortly before the crash. According to the department, the group was leaving a home where they had been participating in the prank when the vehicle struck the woman.Sanchez-Chasmer was arrested and charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, a second-degree felony, police said.Following the woman's death, police said they anticipate the State Attorney's Office will pursue enhanced or additional charges as appropriate based on the circumstances and the outcome of the investigation.Police did not identify the woman in Wednesday's news release.

A Port St. Lucie homeowner says recent heavy rain is worsening damage left behind by Hurricane Milton more than two years ago, as she continues waiting for repairs through the state's Rebuild Florida Housing Repair and Replacement Program. A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV documents unrepaired storm damage and work needed inside her home.WATCH: Recent rainfall worsens Hurricane Milton damage at Port St. Lucie homeCaryn McGregor contacted WPTV asking for help as water continued entering her house through the ceiling, windows and vents. During WPTV's visit, rainwater could be seen dripping inside the home."I'm scared my ceiling's gonna come down," McGregor said.Buckets and towels have become a temporary solution while she waits for more permanent repairs."Water is coming in our house, and we're experiencing so much now," McGregor said. "I just can't believe the events that are happening."Assessment documents unrepaired Hurricane Milton damageMcGregor said her roof was damaged when Hurricane Milton struck Florida in October 2024. She said she initially contacted her insurance company but couldn't afford the deductible and later sought help through Rebuild Florida.A repair assessment reviewed by WPTV lists Oct. 9, 2024, as the date of loss and says McGregor's home was inspected Jan. 6, 2026.The assessment documents unrepaired storm damage and says McGregor reported plumbing problems since the hurricane. The proposed scope of work includes repairs involving ceilings, walls, plumbing, siding, appliances, drywall and doors.The document helps establish the damage identified during the Rebuild Florida assessment, but it does not establish whether the proposed repairs were ultimately approved or funded.Recent rain adds to homeowner's concernsMcGregor told WPTV the continued water intrusion has left her worried that parts of the ceiling could collapse."I can't even have my son living here because the ceiling, I'm scared of it falling on him and hurting him," McGregor said. She also expressed concerns about water and mold.McGregor said water has damaged appliances in the home, including her washer, dryer and dishwasher."The water is ruining everything," she said.Homeowner says she's waiting on permits and repairsMcGregor said Rebuild Florida inspected the home in January but the repairs have not been completed."They were supposed to help," she said. "However they were going to rebuild or replace it, they were supposed to do that."McGregor said she has been told the project is waiting on permits before work can move forward. The documents reviewed by WPTV do not establish which permits remain outstanding, when they were requested or when construction is expected to begin.For McGregor, recent rainfall has added urgency to a problem she says has already kept her family from returning to normal."I want them to help us fix our house," she said. "They said they were going to."WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache reached out to Rebuild Florida seeking answers about the delay, the permitting process and when work could begin. Rebuild Florida acknowledged receiving WPTV's request, but a response addressing those questions had not been received by the time of reporting.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

As the threat of another round of November rain and flooding takes aim at Florida's east coast, many local governments are once again preparing for what may be ahead. "I think everybody is well aware now that this storm drain system was not designed for the flooding we're getting nowadays," St. Lucie County spokesman Erick Gill said.WATCH REPORT BELOW: He said crews are being deployed across the county as they were two weeks ago. "There were probably 50 to 100 staff members out there, including crews in public works, out in the field working during the storm. That's unbudgeted overtime," Gill said. This week, the county offered free sand, donated by Dickerson Infrastructure and Stewart Materials, for residents to bag. Other services cost money, and Gill said budgeting is already on the minds of county leaders now that the Amendment 3 tax cuts are coming. What is uncertain is how the loss of revenue will affect things like storm preparation and response. "We still don't know what the total impacts will be for, you know, with Amendment 3 with the additional homestead exemption," Gill said. "We're looking at the early estimates in this next upcoming fiscal year to be about a $60 million shortfall and then about $120 million once the exemption goes up."

An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after Port St. Lucie Police Department investigators say he struck a 24-year-old woman riding an electric scooter to work and left the scene, leaving her critically injured. Police say the driver had been playing a "ding-dong-ditch" prank with friends shortly before Monday morning's crash.WATCH: E-Scooter Hit-and-Run in Port St. LuciePolice identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer. He was arrested on a felony charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, according to the department.The crash happened near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace. Investigators said the woman was traveling west on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard and had entered a crosswalk when she was hit by a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said Tuesday the woman remained unconscious and in critical condition."We're deeply concerned for her recovery, and our thoughts are with her loved ones," Niemczyk said.Police said a witness stopped to help the woman, called 911 and was able to get the SUV's license plate information. Investigators used that information to identify the vehicle and the driver. Investigators said Sanchez-Chasmer had two friends with him and had been playing "ding-dong-ditch" shortly before the crash. "They were specifically playing, I'll call it ring and run, ding-dong-ditch, at a house that belonged to a friend of theirs, and apparently the mother came to the door and they fled the scene," Niemczyk told WPTV.Niemczyk said investigators believe the people inside the SUV realized a collision had occurred."They're aware that they hit something. I'll say that," he said.According to Niemczyk, Sanchez-Chasmer and the two passengers did not call 911.Niemczyk said the decision to leave the scene was key to the criminal investigation."Had they remained on scene, provided aid, it would have been a very different criminal outcome," Niemczyk said. "There probably wouldn't have been criminal charges at that point."Sanchez-Chasmer was charged with leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury. According to published reports citing law enforcement records, he was being held on a $5,000 bond. Police have not announced charges against the two passengers. WPTV returned to the intersection after the crash and spoke with 15-year-old John Rogalewski, who said he rides an e-scooter to school and is sometimes on the road early in the morning."I'm looking at my surroundings almost the whole time," Rogalewski said. "I'm making sure every time I have to cross the street that there's not a car coming up, and that it is my sign to go, no matter how long I have to wait to cross."Police said the 24-year-old woman was wearing a helmet when she was struck.The investigation remains active, according to police, and toxicology results are still pending.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. An 18-year-old driver has been arrested after a hit-and-run crash critically injured a 24-year-old woman on an electric scooter in Port St. Lucie, police said.WATCH: Update from Chief Leo NiemczykThe incident happened Monday morning near Southwest Gatlin Boulevard and Southwest Feather Terrace, Port St. Lucie police said.According to investigators, the victim was riding an electric scooter westbound on the sidewalk toward Southwest Rosser Boulevard. As the woman on the scooter entered the crosswalk, she was struck by the 18-year-old driver of a gray Chevrolet Tahoe making a left turn onto Southwest Feather Terrace.Police said the driver fled the scene and failed to stop to render aid to the woman.The Port St. Lucie Police Department's Traffic Homicide Investigations Unit identified the driver as Tristan Sanchez-Chasmer and located the vehicle through its investigation. Investigators learned Sanchez-Chasmer had been playing "ding dong ditch" just before the crash.He was arrested on a charge of leaving the scene of a crash involving serious bodily injury, police said.

St. Lucie Public Schools will close all schools and district offices Wednesday, Nov. 18, as officials prepare for the potential for significant rainfall and localized flooding.The district announced the closure Tuesday, saying forecasts from the National Weather Service still have some uncertainty surrounding the exact timing, location and amount of rainfall.However, with the ground already saturated across the community, district leaders said they are taking a cautious approach in the interest of students, families and employees.All after-school activities, aftercare programs and athletic events scheduled for Wednesday are also canceled.District officials said they will monitor rainfall, flooding and road closures throughout the day Wednesday. They will also evaluate access to schools, bus stops and transportation routes.A decision on whether schools will reopen Thursday, Nov. 19, is expected to be announced Wednesday evening.The district said updates will be posted on the official St. Lucie Public Schools website and its social media channels.A flood watch is in effect for the entire Treasure Coast through Friday evening.

All schools in the School District of Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, due to localized flooding, saturated ground and the potential for additional heavy rain.ADDITIONAL CLOSURES: Palm Beach County schools to close Friday amid heavy rain, flood watches St. Lucie County schools closed Friday as heavy rain threatens morning commuteThe district announced the closure Thursday afternoon, citing increasing road closures, particularly in Vero Lake Estates.Rising water at the North County Transportation compound has also forced the district to move school buses.Schools will remain closed next week for Thanksgiving break, Nov. 23-27.The district said schools are scheduled to reopen Monday, Nov. 30.

Indian River County’s Tax Collector and Property Appraiser have formed Task Force 3, to get the word out for residents to qualify the new Homestead Exemption coming with Amendment 3.“What people really need to understand is, there's less than five weeks to get a driver's license to become a resident of the state of Florida,” said Property Appraiser Wesley Davis.WATCH: Amendment 3 task force tries to get the message to Florida residentsFlorida residency is a key component to being able to qualify for the exemption, which is rising to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, after voters approved the referendum on election day.New homeowners coming into the state after January 1, 2027 will have to wait five years for the new full exemptions.Current renters in Florida can still qualify for the new exemption on any future home they buy.“The sense of urgency right now is that you don't need to have a homestead by the end of the year,” Davis says. “What you need to do to qualify for the homestead exemption is you must be a resident of the state of Florida by the end of the year."“That also includes current residents who have failed to get a Florida ID and still hold a driver's license from their previous state,” says Tax Collector Carole Jean Jordan. “They can establish residency in an apartment, and then when they buy a home, they can file for homestead.”The local officials also pointed out county offices will be closed around the upcoming holidays.The impact of Amendment 3 will be felt in future county budgets, and both department heads acknowledge there are already discussions about budgeting next year.Estimates are that the county could lose about 20-30 million dollars over the first couple of years under the amendment.“This will not end property taxes,” Davis says. “About half of everybody's tax bill goes to education, and education is not affected by this at all.”

All School District of Indian River County public schools and district offices will be closed Thursday, Nov. 19, because of expected heavy rain and potential flooding, district officials announced Wednesday. Officials cited already saturated ground and concerns about whether students and employees could safely travel to and from schools.The storm system is expected to affect Indian River, Brevard and Volusia counties between 3 a.m. and 3 p.m. Thursday, according to the district.Indian River County remains under a flood watch as another round of rain moves through the Treasure Coast. The National Weather Service forecast calls for a 95% chance of precipitation Thursday, with about 1.74 inches of rain possible.The district said saturated conditions were a key factor in its decision to cancel classes and close offices."With ground conditions already saturated, we cannot be confident that students and staff will be able to travel safely to and from school," the district said. "Weather conditions may also affect staff members' ability to report to work."The closure comes about two weeks after prolonged rainfall caused significant flooding in Indian River County.A flood watch for Indian River County remains in effect through Friday evening. The National Weather Service is also reporting a high surf advisory and rip current statement for the area.Indian River County officials have warned residents that roads not officially listed as closed could still have standing water or other hazards. Drivers should obey barricades and never attempt to drive through floodwater.The school district said student, family and employee safety remains its highest priority.Officials will continue monitoring conditions and said any additional information will be released through official district communication channels.This story has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Residents in Indian River County are dealing with another round of flooding, with approximately 12 roads closed Thursday evening and the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urging drivers to stay off the roads as water continues to impact neighborhoods.The latest flooding comes just weeks after another round of high water left parts of the Treasure Coast struggling with similar conditions. Residents say this time, however, some neighborhoods appear to have fared better.WATCH: Indian River County residents navigate another round of floodingFor Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, the flooding is an unwelcome reminder of what comes with living in Florida.“I escaped the snow to this,” Holly said.Water has surrounded parts of his neighborhood, Vero Lake Estates, leaving some residents with limited ways to get around.“We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said.Holly said he and other residents previously dropped their flood insurance policies. But after experiencing repeated flooding, he is reconsidering that decision.“We all dropped it. And we haven’t had it since, but now I’m going to rethink it again,” he said.County officials report multiple road closures along Vero Lake Estates. The Sheriff’s Office is urging drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads.Holly said he has not seen vehicles become stranded during this latest round of flooding, unlike the previous event. However, he warned that smaller vehicles may struggle to get through standing water.“The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” he said.Marjorie Hale said she believes this round of flooding has been handled better than the previous one, with more precautions being taken.But she is concerned about drivers who continue traveling too quickly through flooded neighborhoods.“You’ve got a lot of people who just don’t know how to drive in floodwaters,” Hale said.She also worries about the impact waves from passing vehicles can have on nearby homes, particularly older properties.Hale’s neighborhood experienced flooding during the previous round, too. A comparison of conditions outside her home then and now shows how the water has changed.She said drivers should slow down and consider the people living along those flooded streets.Indian River County Public Schools will be closed Friday as flooding continues to affect the area.For some families, the closure means an early start to Thanksgiving break. Hale said her daughter is old enough to stay home while she goes to work.She is also trying to find some humor in the situation.“We get our own private island. That’s what happens when it floods 6 inches of rainfall,” Hale said.Even her dog knows to be cautious around the water.“I let my dog out. He doesn’t wander off because he’s not willing to get in the floodwaters. Smart dog,” she said.While some residents are finding ways to make the best of the situation, Hale recognizes that other families across the Treasure Coast are dealing with more serious flooding and damage to their homes.Her message to the community is simple: look out for one another.“Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” Hale said.She hopes the latest flooding will bring people together, especially those who may need a helping hand.“So let’s join together as a community,” she said.For updated information on Indian River County public road closures, click here.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

A historic Vero Beach neighborhood is getting a new life through art, as sculptor Ross Power leads an effort to transform Edgewood into a vibrant community of artists, galleries, studios and public gathering spaces.Known as the "Father of the Vero Beach Art Village," Power is helping turn a once-overlooked neighborhood into a destination for creativity, where artists can live, work and share their talents.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The transformation is already underway, with murals, public art and community projects taking shape. Power says more galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are in the works, bringing new opportunities for artists, residents and visitors.A historic Vero Beach neighborhood becomes a canvasUnder the shade of a century-old lychee tree, Power reads from a poem dedicated to the tree as a dancer performs beneath its branches."A place where you and me can become we," Power said.For the longtime sculptor, the tree represents something bigger: a gathering place where art can bring people together.That vision is unfolding in Edgewood, a neighborhood established in 1916 that was once home to Vero Beach's first public school and first motel, according to the Vero Beach Art Village organization.Over the years, parts of the neighborhood fell into disrepair. But where others saw aging properties and neglected alleyways, Power saw potential."It spoke to me, and I heard I was once great and now I have fallen into disrepair and not respected at all, and I said we're going to change that," Power told WPTV anchor Meghan McRoberts during a tour of the neighborhood.Power has spent decades creating art and helping develop artistic communities, including an art center in Miami.Now, he's bringing that experience to Vero Beach, with an entire neighborhood as his canvas.Turning Edgewood's alleyways into works of artOne of Power's biggest ambitions is transforming 11 alleyways throughout Edgewood into colorful destinations filled with murals and public art."I'm taking the alleys which are the ugliest part of the neighborhood and turning them into mural opportunities where the alleys are going to be like unbelievable for people to come and visit," Power said."There's a lack of buildings but there's not a lack of fences."Power sees those fences, walls and underused spaces as opportunities to showcase local artists and create an outdoor art experience.But the effort goes beyond beautifying back streets.Special zoning allows artists to live and work in the villageThe city of Vero Beach has established Cultural Arts Village zoning districts designed to encourage artistic businesses while preserving Edgewood's historic residential character.According to the city and the Vero Beach Art Village organization, the zoning creates opportunities for art galleries, studios, live-work spaces and other businesses, depending on the property's classification and applicable approvals.The goal is to create a walkable neighborhood where historic homes can become studios and galleries, and artists can collaborate with their neighbors.“I’ve been working on a bunch of different paintings. And we have projects; there's a bunch of different projects we’ve been working on whether it’s for the city or for trying to save big blue, or our community garden, “ said Linwood Addison Fuller IV, an artist who moved to Edgewood for the focus on art. His wife is also an artist.“It’s so much better to be an artist in a community with other artists,” said sculptor Andrew Draminski. “I’m sitting here working and my neighbors are walking their dog down the alley and come on in and we have a cup of coffee or something like that.”The village's vision extends beyond traditional galleries. Organizers hope to create spaces for music, dance, poetry, photography, workshops and other community events.More galleries, studios and community spaces plannedAccording to the nonprofit Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village, the neighborhood's transformation is a grassroots effort involving artists, residents, businesses and volunteers.The organization highlights ongoing initiatives involving murals, public art, studios, galleries, streetscape improvements and community events.Power says additional galleries, studios, cafes and bed-and-breakfasts are also in the works.For him, the goal isn't simply to attract visitors. It's to create a community where artists can thrive together and residents can take pride in their neighborhood."If you want to eat great food, hear great music, see great things, meet great artists, this is the place," Power said.And beneath the sprawling branches of that century-old lychee tree, Power hopes the community he's helping cultivate will continue to grow.Where is the Vero Beach Art Village?The Vero Beach Art Village is located in the historic Edgewood neighborhood, just west of downtown Vero Beach.The neighborhood generally stretches between 14th and 20th avenues and 18th and 20th streets.The Friends of the Vero Beach Art Village nonprofit encourages residents and visitors to support the effort through volunteering, donations and participation in community art projects.Click here for more information about the village, its projects and opportunities to get involved.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

The School District of Indian River County will operate on a modified schedule Tuesday as a precaution ahead of expected rain and the potential for heavier rainfall.The district announced the schedule change Monday afternoon for Tuesday, Nov. 17.Under the modified-day schedule, extracurricular activities will conclude by 2:30 p.m.Extended Day will be available Tuesday morning but will be closed Tuesday afternoon, according to the district. The district said families should make decisions based on the conditions in their area. If weather conditions prevent a student from attending school, the resulting absence will be excused.Rain is expected Tuesday, with heavier rainfall possible Tuesday evening. The district also warned that heavier rainfall could continue Wednesday through Friday.The School District of Indian River County said additional updates will be provided by 1 p.m. the day before any additional schedule changes.Families should continue monitoring official district communications for the latest information.

Interstate 95 in Indian River County was shut down in both directions early Friday morning, creating a major traffic disruption for drivers near the Indian River-St. Lucie County line.WATCH: Lt. Indiana Miranda gives update after man dies in trooper-involved shooting incidentOn Thursday, at about 11:20 p.m., FHP said a trooper was involved in a shooting incident on I-95 near mile marker 141. According to FHP, the incident began when the trooper initiated a traffic stop for a man driving over 90 mph near mile marker 138. Another trooper joined as back up and that's when, FHP said, the man got aggressive and was uncooperative. "The primary trooper who completed the stop addressed the driver and advised him the reason for the stop was the speed, asked him for his driver's license and registration, he noticed that the driver was hostile," Lt. Indiana Miranda said during a press conference on Friday. "There was a little bit of back and forth between the two, at which point the driver says, 'I don't want to talk to you,' and there was cursing by the driver to our primary trooper."The second trooper stepped in, asking for the man's driver's license as well. That is when the man accelerated and fled the traffic stop, resulting in a pursuit. The pursuit escalated, when the suspect fired a gun at troopers, with one of the troopers returning fire."He said over the radio that there were shots being fired at them. Our trooper returned fire, while driving his vehicle and he was able to engage in a PIT," Miranda said.FHP said the officers used a PIT maneuver causing the suspect to crash and rollover. Authorities said no troopers were injured during the shooting. The suspect was pronounced dead at the scene. FHP initially said the suspect sustained injuries from what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. However, during the 2 p.m. press conference, FHP said that it is not clear who fired the shot that killed the suspect and that is under investigation.FHP said the Florida Department of Law Enforcement is investigating and the two FHP troopers are currently on paid administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation.All northbound and southbound lanes of I-95 were closed for several hours into the morning. All lanes have since reopened.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce boxing gym earns three state champions, second-place team finish
hero.body:
A Future Worth Fighting 4 in Fort Pierce finished with three state champions, a silver medalist and second place overall at the 2026 Florida State Police Athletic League tournament. The boxing gym also ties participation to a daily requirement for its young athletes: They must attend school every day.

Owner Darrion Henry, a teacher at Dan McCarty, said that rule gives students a reason to show up for class. “I’m a teacher at Dan McCarty, so I can see how their behavior has changed, and now I have a lot of kids who show up to school because they know if they don’t show up to school, I’m going to get on them,” Henry said.

Children come to the gym after school to learn boxing. Justice Henry, who has boxed since he was eight, credits the gym’s family-like atmosphere and tough-love environment for his success. “This gym has been the biggest part of my life. I’ve been boxing since I was eight years old, and this became a home for our own little community and us, with everyone we bring in here,” he said.

hero.headline: Martin County approves $200,000 study of Jensen Beach flooding and future risks
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners unanimously approved $200,000 for a study to model the recent flooding in Jensen Beach and identify ways to reduce future flood risks. The study will examine how water moved through the Savannas Preserve area during the storm, which left homes and roads underwater in parts of Jensen Beach earlier this month.

Some residents have questioned whether water discharged into the Blackwell Reservoir, which drains into the Savannas Preserve, contributed to the flooding. Public Works Director James Gorton said the county-funded hydraulic model will have two main objectives: reconstructing the recent storm event and examining potential solutions to reduce flood risk. Before modeling the storm, the county will update the model to account for development to the north, Gorton said. The work will help identify weaknesses during the storm.

The initiative follows a separate county study of areas that have repeatedly flooded. Engineering permit manager and floodplain coordinator Christine Madsen said that analysis identified 53 repetitive loss areas. “We determined what some of the potential causes of the flooding were, and we used it to identify different projects that we could take and move forward within the future,” Madsen said.

The earlier study includes a photo of flooding in the St. Lucie Settlement area along SW Salerno Road, where eight homes were elevated above the 100-year flood elevation with assistance from FEMA. Another photo shows one of the completed homes. “Flood losses are terrible. Just 1 inch of water can majorly impact a property. I mean it can cause up to $25,000 worth of damage,” Madsen said.

Residents can review the analysis of repeatedly flooded areas on the county’s website. Those with questions can call the county at 772-288-5956.

hero.headline: Four arrested after alleged attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club
hero.body:
Four people from Jacksonville, including a 16-year-old, were arrested after an alleged attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The agency is asking residents to review security footage and check their homes and vehicles as investigators determine whether other properties were targeted.

Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the incident began just after 3 a.m., when a family's 17-year-old son heard a suspicious noise outside the home and alerted his parents. The family reviewed security footage and noticed one camera was not working properly. Looking back through earlier recordings, they saw three people circling the house, Budensiek said. Video showed someone placing a sticker over a camera lens near the back door, blocking its view. The family called 911.

Investigators said the group had parked near the C-23 Canal before walking into the gated community. Deputies checked a parking lot near the canal and found a vehicle. One person was taken into custody near it, while the others fled, according to the sheriff. Deputies established a perimeter and searched with help from aviation units, K-9 units and the Stuart Police Department. Two suspects were found hiding beneath the bridge carrying Murphy Road over the C-23 Canal. Budensiek said they were the last two apprehended after the extensive overnight search.

The adults arrested were identified as Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr., Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews and Cameron Elijah Mapson, all 21. A 16-year-old was also arrested. All four face attempted home invasion charges, according to the sheriff's office. Wise also faces charges of grand theft of a firearm and possession of a firearm by a convicted felon. Investigators recovered masks, gloves and a stolen handgun with an extended magazine. Budensiek said the handgun was found as investigators retraced the route between the vehicle and the family's home.

Investigators are examining digital evidence to establish why the group traveled from Jacksonville to Palm City. Residents who discover missing property or signs of a break-in are asked to contact the Martin County Sheriff's Office at 772-220-7060.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie expects temporary Lakehurst Drive repair next week after flood damage
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie expects a temporary repair to Lakehurst Drive sometime next week, three weeks after flooding opened a hole in the road. Two city streets remain closed indefinitely because of infrastructure damage, and repeated rain and shortages of repair materials have slowed the work, city spokesperson Scott Samples said.

Lakehurst Drive is closed between Sandia Drive and Prinville Street. The other closure is Ann Arbor between Pier Court and Jerico Lane. Samples said the early November storm forced five road closures in the city. Crews prioritize repairs based on the severity of the damage and how many people depend on each road.

The hole on Lakehurst Drive is about five feet wide and opened during the Nov. 2 storm that flooded much of St. Lucie County. Frances Bertino, who has lived on the street for nearly 30 years, said it has kept her from turning right out of her driveway for three weeks. Barricades initially blocked her driveway but were later moved back. She now turns around and drives out the other way. City crews arrived Wednesday afternoon to inspect the hole.

“The long-term fixes may take a little bit longer, but our goal is to try to get those temporary fixes in place as quickly as we can to make sure that people have access in and out of their homes,” Samples said.

Wednesday’s Flood Watch was the third the city had prepared for since the start of the month. Samples said flooding along Florida’s east coast has left many communities seeking the same repair materials at once, making supplies harder to obtain.

The National Weather Service in Melbourne has St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee and Brevard counties under a Flood Watch until 1 a.m. Thursday. Forecasters expect 1 to 3 inches of rain, with 4 to 5 inches or more possible in some places. Heavy rain on already soaked ground could flood roads and low-lying areas.

President Donald Trump approved Florida’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration for flooding that began Oct. 31, making FEMA individual assistance available in St. Lucie, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and Brevard counties. The aid can help pay for temporary housing, home repairs and uninsured property losses. FEMA says families should file insurance claims first, then apply at DisasterAssistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362. Homeowners, renters and small businesses can also apply for low-interest SBA disaster loans.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie man gets 47 months in prison for $260K AI cryptocurrency fraud
hero.body:
David Anthony Sanchez, 36, of Port St. Lucie, was sentenced to 47 months in federal prison and ordered to pay restitution for a cryptocurrency fraud scheme that used an AI-generated voice to impersonate online streamer N3ON and cost victims about $260,000. Sanchez pleaded guilty to money laundering and aggravated identity theft, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Federal prosecutors said Sanchez convinced organizers of a cryptocurrency memecoin project that N3ON had agreed to endorse and participate in it. According to court records, Sanchez created online accounts designed to look as though they belonged to N3ON and communicated with organizers while posing as both the streamer and his representative. He also executed agreements using N3ON's identity and sent organizers an AI-generated recording that mimicked the streamer's voice to falsely confirm his participation, prosecutors said.

Believing those representations were legitimate, the victims transferred approximately $260,000 in cryptocurrency to accounts Sanchez controlled, according to prosecutors. Authorities said he then converted a substantial portion of the cryptocurrency into U.S. dollars through transactions designed to conceal the money's source and ownership. Prosecutors said Sanchez used the proceeds for his personal benefit.

“Behind every fraud scheme are real people who suffer real financial harm,” Acting U.S. Attorney Yara Lorenzo Klukas said in a release. She said Sanchez exploited artificial intelligence to manipulate victims' trust and take their money. The FBI's Miami Field Office investigated the case.

hero.headline: Stuart warns businesses of fake city invoices seeking thousands in project fees
hero.body:
The City of Stuart is warning businesses and contractors about fraudulent emails seeking thousands of dollars in development, building, planning or project-related fees. Several businesses with active projects and applications have recently reported receiving emails claiming to be from the city, with some recipients instructed to wire funds.

All official City of Stuart development and permitting fees must be paid through the city’s official OpenGov application portal. The city says it does not send invoices by email for these purposes.

One fraudulent email address reported to the city is commissions.stuartfl.gov@usa.com. The city encourages applicants with active projects to remain vigilant and carefully review all correspondence related to their projects to avoid being scammed.

cards.teaser: A truck hauling mulch jackknifed and struck an SUV Tuesday, sending five people to hospitals. All northbound lanes reopened at 1:56 p.m., according to the Florida Highway Patrol.
cards.body:
Five people were transported to hospitals after a truck hauling mulch jackknifed and struck an SUV on Florida's Turnpike in Martin County on Tuesday afternoon. All northbound lanes have reopened, according to the Florida Highway Patrol.

The medium-duty truck was pulling a trailer loaded with pallets of mulch. Both vehicles were traveling northbound when the truck jackknifed, striking a wall and the SUV.

Four people were transported to Florida Coast Medical Center, and one was transported to Martin Memorial South. The Florida Highway Patrol confirmed that the crash involved injuries.

The crash shut down all northbound lanes before they reopened at 1:56 p.m., according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The right shoulder remained blocked as of 3 p.m. Tuesday, according to Florida 511.

hero.headline: Family remembers Alexis Cuellar ahead of funeral after Port St. Lucie hit-and-run
hero.body:
Alexis Cuellar’s family is speaking publicly for the first time about the 24-year-old killed in a Port St. Lucie hit-and-run as they prepare for her funeral service, scheduled for Wednesday, Nov. 25, at Haisley Funeral Home in Fort Pierce. Cuellar, known to her family as Lexi, was riding her scooter to work Nov. 16 when a vehicle struck her near SW Gatlin Boulevard, according to police. She died Nov. 17.

At the family’s Port St. Lucie home, her father, Alberto Vasquez, and relatives, some visiting from Texas, gathered around photos and remembered her life. “Alexis wasn't just a ray of sunshine, you know. I think to us she was just the sun,” Vasquez said. He described his eldest daughter as someone who had cared for others since childhood, beginning with her siblings. She loved children and dreamed of working with them. Vasquez also remembered her time in Junior ROTC with pride.

Her aunt, Minerva Benitez, described the loss the family is grieving. “She was the sweetest person ever, and it's a huge loss for the family,” Benitez said. Vasquez said the support the family has received has helped them through the first difficult days after Cuellar’s death.

On the morning of the crash, Vasquez watched his daughter leave for her job at Wendy’s. She had been excited about picking up more hours. He saw her ride away on her scooter and assumed she would be OK. Five minutes later, he learned there had been a crash. Vasquez said he wished he could have been there to help her and tell her he loved her.

Police have charged 18-year-old Tristian Ray Sanchez-Chasmer with leaving the scene. Investigators say he had been playing ding-dong-ditch with friends before getting behind the wheel of a Chevy Tahoe. He is accused of striking Cuellar while she rode her scooter in a crosswalk, then leaving. Additional charges, including vehicular homicide, could follow as police continue investigating the crash.

hero.headline: Heritage Plantation residents near Vero Beach seek help after repeated flooding
hero.body:
Residents of Heritage Plantation mobile home park near Vero Beach are asking for help after repeated flooding damaged property and complicated emergency access. More heavy rain is forecast, and Indian River County’s Emergency Operations Center is partially activated. Dawn Carboni, the community’s HOA president, said residents are frightened after battling multiple floods this month. “They just want to feel safe in their homes,” she said.

Resident Joe Waters recorded video Saturday evening outside his mobile home as a car drove through floodwaters that nearly covered its headlights. He said wakes from passing vehicles struck and toppled bricks protecting his home’s undercarriage. “The water came up probably about thigh high,” Waters said. “Came up into the driveway, went into the house.” Waters and his wife were able to clean their home, but he said his car remained in the shop with $4,600 in damage, awaiting insurance company approval.

Carboni said the flooding has created dangerous conditions for emergency responders. During one medical call, an EMS crew had to park on 82nd Avenue because it could not reach a resident’s home, she said. A large fire truck then had to reach the home. Carboni said she wants to speak for neighbors who cannot speak up and draw attention to the community’s repeated flooding. “We need help, and we’re asking for help,” she said.

Indian River County emergency managers said they are operating at Level 2, meaning the Emergency Operations Center is partially activated. The county’s state of emergency has been extended through Nov. 30 as the community faces the forecast for more heavy rain.

hero.headline: Four arrested in attempted home invasion at Palm City's Evergreen Club
hero.body:
Four suspects were arrested and charged with attempted home invasion Tuesday at Palm City's Evergreen Club, and the Martin County Sheriff's Office is asking residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in. The suspects, three men and a 16-year-old boy from Jacksonville, are being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. Anyone who finds property missing should call the sheriff's office at 772-220-7060.

The attempted break-in happened around 3 a.m. at a home on SW Bimini Circle in the community off Murphy Road, according to the sheriff's office. A 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside and alerted his parents, who called 911, interrupting the attempt. Sheriff John Budensiek said the suspects tried to enter through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker. Home security video showed the group wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves.

Investigators said the suspects parked along a canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. When deputies arrived, the four ran in different directions, according to the sheriff's office. Deputies established a perimeter with help from the agency's aviation team and K-9 unit, along with the Stuart Police Department. K-9 teams tracked down all four suspects in separate locations throughout the community.

The 16-year-old was found hiding in a bush outside the community, and two men were found under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road. The fourth suspect was found in a nearby parking lot. Detectives believe that person was the getaway driver. The sheriff's office said at least one suspect was armed with a handgun. Deputies recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm.

The adult suspects were identified as Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22; Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21; and Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21. All four suspects face attempted home invasion charges. Wise also faces charges of grand theft and possession of a firearm. Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories.

hero.headline: FEMA aid opens for flood-hit residents in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties
hero.body:
Federal disaster assistance is now available to residents affected by flooding in Indian River, Martin and St. Lucie counties, including grants for temporary housing and home repairs, along with low-cost loans for uninsured property losses. FEMA announced the assistance late Tuesday for individuals and families in those three Treasure Coast counties, as well as Palm Beach, Okeechobee and Brevard counties.

Residents who suffered damage or other losses should first file a claim with their insurance provider, then apply for FEMA assistance at DisasterAssistance.gov, through the FEMA App or by calling 1-800-621-3362. Applicants who use a relay service, including video relay or captioned telephone services, should give FEMA the number for that service when applying. The assistance also includes other programs designed to help people recover from the disaster.

Federal funding is also available on a cost-sharing basis to state, tribal and eligible local governments, as well as certain private nonprofit organizations, for debris removal and emergency protective measures. That assistance covers Palm Beach, Martin, Indian River, Okeechobee, Brevard and Hardee counties.

U.S. Rep. Lois Frankel said the declaration unlocks critical federal recovery resources for residents, businesses and local governments affected by the flooding. She said Palm Beach County officials estimate that $53 million in disaster assistance is needed countywide, including nearly $35 million for individuals and families, plus more than $18 million for local governments’ emergency response and cleanup costs.

hero.headline: Four arrested after alleged armed home invasion attempt at Palm City's Evergreen Club
hero.body:
Four people were arrested after an alleged armed home invasion attempt early Tuesday at Palm City's Evergreen Club, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The agency is asking Palm City residents to check their homes and vehicles for missing property or signs of a break-in.

A 17-year-old boy heard a noise outside his family's home on SW Bimini Circle at 3 a.m. and alerted his parents, who called 911, the sheriff's office said. Investigators said the call interrupted the attempted home invasion at the community off Murphy Road. At least one suspect was armed with a handgun, according to the agency.

Investigators said the suspects parked along a canal and walked half a mile into the neighborhood to target the home. Home security video showed the group around 3 a.m. wearing dark clothing, masks and gloves. Sheriff John Budensiek said they tried to enter through a back door and covered a surveillance camera lens with a sticker.

The four suspects, three men and a 16-year-old boy from Jacksonville, ran in different directions when deputies arrived, the sheriff's office said. Deputies established a perimeter with help from the agency's aviation team, K-9 unit and the Stuart Police Department. K-9s tracked the suspects to separate hiding places. The teenager was found in a bush outside the community, two men were under a nearby bridge off Murphy Road, and the fourth suspect was in a nearby parking lot. Detectives believe the suspect found in the parking lot was the getaway driver.

The suspects were identified as Nathaniel Phillip Wise Jr, 22; Za'kyri Isreal Emmanuel Crews, 21; Cameron Elijah Mapson, 21; and a 16-year-old boy. All four were charged with attempted home invasion and are being held in the Martin County Jail without bond. Wise also faces charges of grand theft and possession of a firearm.

Deputies recovered masks, gloves and a stolen firearm, according to the sheriff's office. Budensiek said three of the four suspects have violent criminal histories.

Palm City residents who find property missing from their homes or vehicles should call the sheriff's office at 772-220-7060.
