hero.headline: Federal disaster request for Martin County flooding remains pending
hero.body:
Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Jared Perdue confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9 following the Nov. 2 flooding in Martin County. The request remains pending as the county estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage. Asked about rebuilding assistance if federal aid is denied, Perdue emphasized coordination with FEMA, nonprofit partnerships and emergency response efforts. A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially provide individual assistance to qualifying residents.

In Jensen Beach, dumpsters line driveways along Hyline Drive, where homes have been stripped to their frames and residents have discarded waterlogged belongings. Linda Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters for nine days before beginning to salvage possessions. Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. Those loans carry repayment requirements and liens, and income limits restrict eligibility.

Commissioner Blake Capps proposed a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall outside existing eligibility requirements. “There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit,” Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding. When asked about help for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but cannot afford repairs, Perdue pointed to National Guard personnel and nonprofit organizations helping remove damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials from homes to help prevent mold growth.

The county also faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, while emergency response expenses are still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said the county could be responsible for those costs if federal reimbursement is denied, potentially requiring officials to redirect budget money or find other funding sources. Perdue said damage assessments would continue to be submitted to FEMA. The state is also responding to another significant rainfall event, and Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance.
hero.article_text: Nearly three weeks after historic flooding forced families from their homes and caused millions of dollars in damage across Martin County, residents are still waiting for a federal disaster declaration that could unlock critical financial assistance. Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

cards.headline: Martin County’s proposed Kanner Highway data center could advance without commission vote
cards.teaser: County officials expect a staff report in December, followed by a public forum. An administrative approval process could allow the project to proceed without a public hearing or commission vote.
cards.body:
A proposed data center off Kanner Highway in Martin County could receive administrative approval without a public hearing or county commission vote, according to county officials. The approval process has become a focus of residents’ opposition after the county canceled a Friday meeting about the development, citing overwhelming public interest.

The county expects to release a staff report examining the project in December, then schedule a public forum where residents can ask questions. That forum will likely include a presentation from the applicant. The updated application calls for approximately 1.6 million square feet of development, including an existing warehouse, west of Interstate 95 and about half a mile from Crystal Lake Elementary School. The initial proposal called for just under 1 million square feet.

Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden said an ordinance adopted in 2010 established administrative approval for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within those classifications. Walden said an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement also covers the proposal and allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. He said the county will review potential impacts before deciding whether to approve the project. “This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted.”

County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers while the county reviews its development regulations. County officials say this application is exempt because it was submitted before the moratorium was proposed. Walden said the code review will consider revisions to give the public more say in future projects.

Residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center on Friday despite the meeting’s cancellation. They have raised concerns about cooling-equipment noise, water and electricity use, wildlife displacement, property values and possible health effects on students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. “We need answers, and we need them quick,” said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from the school.

Walden said the canceled gathering was an informal question-and-answer meeting requested by members of the public, rather than a decision-making session. As interest grew, the county determined it could not accommodate the crowd. He said additional public meetings and workshops will give residents opportunities to ask questions and learn about the proposal.
cards.article_text: A controversial proposal to build a more than 1.6 million-square-foot data center just half a mile from an elementary school is drawing growing opposition in Martin County, where residents are raising concerns about everything from environmental impacts to whether they'll have a say in the project's approval. WATCH: 'We need answers': Martin Co. officials address outrage over proposed data center On Friday morning, a small but vocal group of residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center, demanding answers about the massive development proposed for a parcel of land off Kanner Highway, west of Interstate 95. They had planned to attend a meeting with the county's Growth Management Department. But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest. Residents showed up anyway. "We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School." McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods. "Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking. Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary. Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site. “They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values. "We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this." Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost. But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it. The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online: "This meeting has been canceled. Due to the level of public interest, a more formal meeting will be scheduled and publicly noticed in advance to accommodate any and all residents who wish to attend, learn more, and share their thoughts. Stay tuned to our website and social media as meeting details are finalized." For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration. "The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs. Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation. But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session. Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects. He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center. When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel. "We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." When asked why residents weren't being given more opportunities to weigh in, Walden maintained the county has been transparent. "We are transparent through the process, and everything can be made available to anyone that is interested," he said. Walden said additional public meetings and workshops will be scheduled to allow residents to ask questions and learn more about the project. But the canceled meeting is only one of several controversies surrounding the development. Another major point of contention is the timing of the developer's application. 27, Martin County commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers, temporarily restricting new applications while the county reviews its development regulations. But records show the application for this project was submitted the day before the moratorium was proposed on October 13. That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials. Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications. "They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen." WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns. Neither responded by publication time. Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval. Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners. For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical. Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved. "With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said. "To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School. The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse. Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values. Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development. Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision. He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved. "There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said. "This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted." The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December. Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development. No date for that meeting has been announced. For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land. It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision. The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition. "If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

hero.headline: Indian River County unveils memorial to two deputies killed in line of duty
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a memorial Saturday honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, two deputies killed in the line of duty. The ceremony came on the first anniversary of Sweeting-Mashkow’s death while serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community.

Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for the unveiling outside the sheriff’s office’s new administration building. Bagpipes and taps sounded during the ceremony. The memorial also honors Raczkoski, who was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.

“The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.

Sweeting-Mashkow, 47, was one of three deputies serving the eviction notice on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said Michael Halberstam, 37, retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. David Long, a locksmith who was there for the eviction, was critically wounded and later died from his injuries.

Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death was the second line-of-duty death in the agency’s 100-year history.

“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”

Knott also spoke about the risks officers face at work. “All of these officers that step out into the community, they never know what their day is going to bring,” she said.

Flowers said he hopes the memorial will bear only the two deputies’ names. “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.”

cards.headline: Indian River County flooding closed roads, prompted Friday school closure
cards.teaser: About 12 county roads were closed Thursday evening as floodwaters affected neighborhoods. Indian River County Public Schools announced a Friday closure.
cards.body:
Another round of flooding closed about 12 roads in Indian River County on Thursday evening and prompted Indian River County Public Schools to announce a Friday closure. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads as water affected neighborhoods, including Vero Lake Estates.

County officials reported multiple road closures in Vero Lake Estates, where water surrounded parts of the neighborhood and limited some residents’ travel. The flooding came just weeks after another round of high water affected parts of the Treasure Coast. Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, said his household had stocked up. “We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said.

Holly said he and other residents had previously dropped their flood insurance policies, but the repeated flooding had him reconsidering. “We all dropped it. And we haven’t had it since, but now I’m going to rethink it again,” he said. He also cautioned that smaller vehicles could struggle in the standing water. “The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” Holly said.

Resident Marjorie Hale said she believed the latest flooding had been handled better than the previous round, with more precautions being taken. She remained concerned about motorists driving too quickly through flooded neighborhoods and the waves their vehicles could send toward nearby homes, particularly older properties. “You’ve got a lot of people who just don’t know how to drive in floodwaters,” Hale said. She urged drivers to slow down and consider residents along the streets.

Hale’s neighborhood also flooded during the previous round. She said her daughter was old enough to stay home during the planned school closure while she went to work. With other Treasure Coast families facing flooding and damage to their homes, Hale encouraged neighbors to help one another ahead of the holiday. “Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” she said.

hero.headline: Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveils memorial to two fallen deputies
hero.body:
The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office unveiled a memorial Saturday honoring two deputies killed in the line of duty, marking the first anniversary of Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow’s death. The memorial outside the agency’s new administration building honors Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, whose deaths occurred 40 years apart.

Hundreds of family members, friends, law enforcement officers and community members gathered for the unveiling as bagpipes and taps played. “The two heroes that are on this memorial are two people that our community will remember forever,” Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said.

Sweeting-Mashkow, 47, was one of three deputies serving an eviction notice at a home in the Bermuda Club community on Nov. 21, 2025, when authorities said Michael Halberstam, 37, retrieved a weapon and opened fire. Sweeting-Mashkow was killed, and Deputy Florentino Arizpe was shot in the shoulder. David Long, a locksmith there for the eviction, was critically wounded and later died from his injuries.

Sweeting-Mashkow had served with the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office for more than 25 years. Her death was the second line-of-duty death in the agency’s 100-year history. Raczkoski was killed in the line of duty 40 years ago.

“It’s an honor to be out here but also very sad,” community member Joanne Knott said. “To think that it happened a year ago is strange because it feels like it was yesterday.”

Flowers said he hopes the memorial will bear only the two names it now holds. “I hope we never have to add names to this memorial again.”

hero.headline: Indian River County unveils monument honoring two fallen deputies
hero.teaser: The tribute honors Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski. Saturday’s unveiling marked one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed during an eviction call near Vero Beach.
hero.body:
A monument honoring Sgt. Terri Sweeting-Mashkow and Deputy Richard Raczkoski was unveiled Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, marking one year since Sweeting-Mashkow was killed during an eviction call near Vero Beach. Family, friends, colleagues and community leaders gathered for the unveiling.

Sweeting-Mashkow, a 25-year veteran, was shot and killed on November 21, 2025, while deputies were serving an eviction notice at a home in the gated Bermuda Club community. Investigators said Michael Halberstam opened fire, killing Sweeting-Mashkow and wounding Deputy Tino Arizpe. Locksmith David Long also was shot and later died at the hospital. Deputies returned fire, and Halberstam died the following day.

“Terri was an amazing deputy. She had a beautiful heart, and she will be missed,” Sheriff Eric Flowers said following her death.

Raczkoski was fatally shot on September 23, 1986, while responding to a call at a Vero Beach convenience store. Investigators said William Reaves shot Raczkoski four times as the deputy tried to flee following a struggle over a gun. Reaves, 77, was executed on October 20, 2026, nearly 40 years after the murder.

The monument brings the two deputies’ names together in a permanent tribute nearly four decades after Raczkoski’s death. The sheriff's office said it represents the strength of its law enforcement family and serves as a reminder that those who gave their lives protecting the community will never be forgotten.

hero.headline: Florida emergency director confirms Martin County disaster aid request remains pending
hero.body:
Florida’s Nov. 9 request for an expedited federal disaster declaration following Martin County’s flooding remains pending, Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Jared Perdue confirmed. Asked about rebuilding help if federal assistance is denied, Perdue pointed to nonprofit partnerships and emergency personnel helping clean out flooded homes. Martin County estimates about $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage from flooding that began Nov. 2. A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially provide individual assistance to qualifying residents.

“We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth,” Perdue said. He said the state continues to assess damage and submit information to FEMA. Meanwhile, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million through Florida’s State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. Those loans carry repayment requirements and liens, and the program’s income limits restrict eligibility. Commissioner Blake Capps proposed a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall outside existing aid requirements.

On Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, Linda Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 SHIP grant after flooding severely damaged her home. She and her neighbors navigated waist-deep water for nine days before they could begin salvaging their belongings. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged possessions have been discarded, and homes have been stripped to their frames. “Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home,” Weisbecker said. She lost family photographs and belongings collected over decades.

The county also faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said the county could have to cover those costs if federal reimbursement is denied, potentially requiring officials to redirect budget money or find other funding. Perdue said the state has activated the National Guard and partnered with nonprofits to remove damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials from homes to help prevent mold growth. He said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance, as crews also respond to another significant rainfall event affecting Florida communities.

Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. hero.headline: Indian River County flood watch canceled as road, school closures continued Friday
hero.body:
The National Weather Service canceled a Flood Watch for Indian River County Friday morning, while flooding and roadway damage continued to affect roads across the county. The School District of Indian River County remained closed for the day.

Additional showers remained possible, with the heaviest rainfall threat farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials urged drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

Friday’s road closures included 130th Street; 79th Street west of 130th Avenue, where a roadway washout forced the closure; and 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW, which was closed because of roadway damage. In Vero Lake Estates, closures affected 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues.

Partial blockages affected U.S. 1 near Barber Street, 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation and Skyline Drive from Periwinkle to Barber Street. Old Dixie Highway SW had flooding and partial blockages at several locations. The county said these were selected locations and directed drivers to its live road closure map for additional closures and updates.

Officials said water needs time to recede and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews were working in affected areas, and drivers were asked to give them room and follow barricades.

The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center were open Friday. Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remained closed. School district updates are available on the district website.

The county also said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding was greater.

hero.headline: Florida's disaster request remains pending as Martin County flood victims seek aid
hero.body:
Florida Division of Emergency Management Director Jared Perdue confirmed the state's Nov. 9 request for an expedited federal disaster declaration remains pending as Martin County families struggle to rebuild after the Nov. 2 flooding. Asked about rebuilding assistance for homeowners who cannot qualify for existing aid, Perdue pointed to nonprofit partnerships and emergency personnel helping clean out flooded homes.

Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage. A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially provide individual assistance to qualifying residents. FEMA confirmed the request remained under review. Perdue said the state continues to assess damage and submit information to the agency.

Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. Resident Linda Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters for nine days before they could begin salvaging belongings. Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. She lost family photographs and possessions accumulated over decades. “You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?” Weisbecker said.

Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. Those loans carry repayment requirements and liens, and income restrictions limit eligibility. Commissioner Blake Capps proposed a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall outside existing aid limits. “There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit,” Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting.

Perdue said the state activated the National Guard and is partnering with nonprofits to remove damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials from flooded homes to help prevent mold growth. He also said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance.

The county also faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess said Martin County could have to cover those costs if federal reimbursement is denied, potentially requiring officials to redirect budget money or find other funding sources.

cards.headline: Investigation into alleged misconduct involving child at Stuart hospital suspended
cards.teaser: A newly released Martin County Sheriff's Office report says the investigation was suspended pending additional interviews with the child and witnesses.
cards.body:
A Martin County Sheriff's Office investigation into alleged inappropriate conduct involving a child at a Stuart hospital was suspended pending additional interviews with the child and witnesses, according to a recently released case report. The allegations concern an Oct. 16, 2026, incident at Cleveland Clinic South on Southeast Salerno Road.

Investigators identified the suspect as James Ryan Colby, 47. The report lists Colby as the subject of an investigation into a charge of promoting sexual activity involving a victim younger than 16.

According to investigators, a hospital employee monitoring a live-stream camera reported witnessing the alleged incident involving the child. The report states that a nurse later went to the hospital room and instructed those involved to leave.

The allegations were initially reported to the Stuart Police Department. Investigators determined that the incident occurred outside the department's jurisdiction, and the case was referred for further investigation. Sheriff's deputies received information from a Stuart Police Department report and a Florida Department of Children and Families report. One witness told investigators she did not observe inappropriate conduct. Authorities said the child later disclosed information during a follow-up contact. The report states that additional interviews with the child and witnesses were pending when the investigation was suspended.

hero.headline: Indian River County plans monument unveiling for two deputies killed in line of duty
hero.teaser: The ceremony honoring Sgt. Terri Jean Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski is scheduled for 10 a.m. Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office.
hero.body:
A monument honoring Sgt. Terri Jean Sweeting-Mashkow and Cpl. Richard Raczkoski, two Indian River County sheriff’s deputies killed in the line of duty, is scheduled to be unveiled at 10 a.m. Saturday at the Indian River County Sheriff’s Office.

The memorial will stand in front of the agency’s new building. Sheriff Eric Flowers said the monument will give the public a place on the sheriff’s office campus to remember the deputies. “The public will have a place on our campus to come and see those two that have lost their lives, and it will be there forever for them to always be memorialized there in front of our new building,” Flowers said.

The ceremony is planned to mark the first anniversary of Sweeting-Mashkow’s death. She was killed while serving an eviction notice at a home along Governor’s Way. Investigators said Michael Halberstam opened fire, fatally shooting her.

Raczkoski was killed in September 1986 after being shot at a convenience store near Vero Beach. William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski, was executed last month after receiving the death penalty.

Now, after a WPTV report on the delays and growing frustration among flood victims, Florida's top emergency management official is responding to questions about the state's recovery efforts—and what help families can expect if FEMA funding never arrives. Watch more from Kate Hussey: In an exclusive interview with WPTV investigative reporter Kate Hussey, Jared Perdue, director of the Florida Division of Emergency Management, confirmed the state submitted an expedited federal disaster declaration request Nov. 9, one week after the initial flooding. But nearly two weeks after that request, a decision remains pending. "We've been very engaged with FEMA, and we did actually submit an expedited disaster declaration request to FEMA on November the ninth," Perdue said. "FEMA has been very closely coordinating with us in reviewing that, and I'm sure they're going to make quick work of it." The uncertainty comes as Martin County estimates approximately $18 million in residential and public infrastructure damage, with families still struggling to afford repairs and another round of historic rainfall complicating recovery efforts. Along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach, the devastation is still visible. Dumpsters line driveways, waterlogged belongings have been discarded and homes have been stripped down to their frames. For Linda Weisbecker, whose home was among those severely damaged, the destruction has been overwhelming. "It's like an apocalypse here," Weisbecker told WPTV in an earlier interview. For nine days, Weisbecker and her neighbors navigated waist-deep floodwaters before they could begin salvaging what remained of their homes. "Once we got through that and the water came out, we just all started pitching in, going in to see what we can salvage from each home," she said. But much of what Weisbecker lost cannot be replaced. Our house is empty," she said. "We lost everything, from pictures of our children and their lives, our friends, our grandkids, now we have great-grandkids. Everything [my husband] had since he was 13 on is gone." Weisbecker has been approved for a $25,000 grant through Florida's State Housing Initiatives Partnership, or SHIP, program. But for families facing tens of thousands of dollars in repairs, that assistance may cover only a fraction of the cost. And not everyone will qualify. "You do think about that process and you sit there and you say to yourself, how am I gonna do this?" Weisbecker said. That question is at the center of WPTV's ongoing investigation. Martin County estimates the flooding caused: A federal major disaster declaration could make certain public infrastructure repairs eligible for FEMA reimbursement and potentially open the door to individual assistance for qualifying residents. But approval is not guaranteed. When WPTV initially contacted FEMA, the agency confirmed it had received the disaster declaration request and that it remained under review. FEMA referred additional questions about the response and recovery timeline to the Florida Division of Emergency Management. Hussey subsequently pressed Perdue on what would happen if the federal government denied the request. "If FEMA ultimately denies federal assistance, does Florida have a Plan B, or are these families simply on their own?" Hussey asked. Perdue did not identify a specific alternative state funding program, instead emphasizing Florida's experience responding to natural disasters and its ongoing coordination with federal and local officials. "This is something that we're very used to doing. I mean, in Florida, we deal with natural disasters all the time," Perdue said. "We have a great relationship with FEMA, and usually those things go very well." He added that the state remains focused on immediate response efforts, including search and rescue operations and meeting residents' emergency needs. In the meantime, Martin County is working to distribute approximately $1 million in available SHIP funding to qualifying residents. Eligible homeowners may receive grants of up to $25,000, with additional assistance potentially available through loans of up to $75,000. However, those loans come with repayment requirements and liens. Income eligibility restrictions could also leave some families without assistance, even if they cannot afford to rebuild on their own. "There's going to be a lot of heart-wrenching cases where somebody barely missed the limit," Commissioner Blake Capps said during a recent Martin County Commission meeting. Capps proposed establishing a separate county-funded emergency assistance program for residents who fall through the cracks. But when WPTV asked where that money would come from, Capps acknowledged a funding source had not yet been identified. we'd have to talk to staff," he said. County Human Services Director Michelle Miller previously told commissioners the state had promised additional disaster relief funding, although neither the amount nor the timeline had been confirmed. "They haven't confirmed the amount yet but has assured us we will be getting some disaster relief funds," Miller told Hussey. Hussey raised those concerns directly with Perdue, asking whether the state had other programs available for families who earn too much to qualify for existing assistance but not enough to pay for repairs. Perdue pointed to the state's partnerships with nonprofit organizations and its deployment of emergency personnel to assist with cleanup. "We've actually activated the National Guard, and are also partnering with nonprofits to do what they call the muck and gut of homes that have been flooded," Perdue said. That work includes removing damaged drywall and other waterlogged materials to help prevent mold growth. "We're providing the assistance that we can and partnering with those nonprofit organizations as well," he said. However, Perdue did not identify a specific funding program to cover rebuilding costs for homeowners who do not qualify for existing assistance. The financial uncertainty extends beyond individual homeowners. Martin County faces approximately $15 million in combined beach and road damage, with additional emergency response expenses still being assessed. County spokesperson Martha Ann Kniess previously told WPTV that without federal reimbursement, Martin County could be left responsible for covering those costs, potentially forcing officials to redirect money from elsewhere in the budget or identify other funding sources. Hussey asked Perdue whether the state would help cover those expenses if FEMA denied federal assistance — or whether the financial burden could ultimately fall on local taxpayers. Perdue did not commit to providing state funding for those repairs. "We are and have been doing damage assessments ever since we submitted the first disaster declaration request," he said. "As those damage assessments come in, we'll continue to coordinate with FEMA and make sure all that information is submitted." The state's response follows an emotional Martin County Commission meeting Tuesday, where residents pleaded with elected officials to do more to secure recovery funding. Fight for us!" one resident urged commissioners. Others questioned why families were being asked to wait even longer for answers. "And the answer from this dais is wait 13 more days?!?" another resident asked. Commissioner Eileen Vargas said she had reached out to FEMA through personal contacts in an effort to expedite the process. "I did, through contacts, reach out to FEMA to try and get this going," Vargas said. Vargas also told residents she expected a new FEMA director to take office Nov. 30 and hoped that development could help move the disaster declaration forward. But even if a declaration is approved, not all losses or recovery expenses would necessarily qualify for federal assistance. As Martin County continues to recover from the Nov. 2 flooding, Perdue said the state is also responding to another significant rainfall event affecting communities across Florida. Ron DeSantis expanded the state's emergency executive order to include 21 counties. The state has mobilized resources from the National Guard, State Guard, Florida Highway Patrol and Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, among other agencies. "We're actively still responding to the previous flooding event on November 2, and now we're actively dealing with a current, another historic rain event that's brought record amount of flooding in many counties throughout the state," Perdue said. The overlapping disasters have added urgency to recovery efforts, particularly for residents whose homes remain exposed after being gutted. Perdue said state resources remain available for immediate needs, including food, water, shelter and emergency medical assistance. We're fully mobilized," he said. We're going to be with you till the very end, and we're going to make sure we help everybody get back on their feet." Despite those assurances, several critical questions remain unresolved. FEMA has not announced a decision on Florida's expedited disaster declaration request. The state has not identified a specific alternative rebuilding assistance program for homeowners who do not qualify for existing aid, nor has it committed to covering Martin County's public infrastructure losses if federal funding is denied. For residents like Weisbecker, the uncertainty is more than a question of government funding. It's a question of whether they can afford to return to the homes they've spent years building their lives in. "This is very urgent for people to get back into their daily lives," Weisbecker said. "This is total devastation.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie gets approval to add contractor for swale-liner backlog
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie recently received approval to add a contractor to speed up outstanding swale-liner installations, the city says, as one family reports nearly four years of standing-water problems at its home. Oprah Fasulo and her mother, Divika Todd, say they have now been told installation could take another two years.

The family says water collects around its property even after lighter rainfall and takes days to clear, bringing mosquitoes. Swale liners are designed to help water move rather than remain on properties. Fasulo jokingly calls the standing-water problem a “mosquito hotel.”

Fasulo and Todd trace the problem to when their Port St. Lucie home was built, during changes in responsibility for installing the liners. According to the family, that responsibility shifted from the city to builders and later returned to the city. They say their house was built between those changes and never received a liner.

When the family contacted Port St. Lucie, Fasulo said, they were told the city had to perform the installation. “They said that they have to install it. The homeowners are not allowed to install it,” she said. Fasulo said she understood that requirement but was frustrated by the wait. “I understand that totally, but they told us that it was three years; it would be done,” she said.

Scott Samples said other families are also waiting for installations. “We were recently approved to add a contractor to help us to expedite getting some of these put in,” Samples said. He said the city is also evaluating how to use its available resources to complete outstanding installations more quickly and adjusting its plans as that work proceeds.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie road partially collapses after flooding as neighbor warns of growing hole
hero.body:
A road and nearby property in Port St. Lucie partially collapsed during historic flooding, leaving a hole that a neighbor says has continued to grow each day. The damage developed as floodwater poured into the area and the ground buckled before giving way. Sections of the road and adjoining property fell into the hole, with aerial views showing the extent of the collapse. Yoshi Duran, who lives nearby, pointed out the damage close to her home and described how much of the area had been underwater. “All this was flooded,” she said.

Duran said the widening hole has left her worried about another collapse and what the damage could mean for the homes around it. Her concern is not just about the road that has already fallen away, but also about whether more ground could give way as the hole expands. “It’s not anything to laugh about. It is a dangerous situation because they’re not knowing when it can cave in,” Duran said. She said the hole has grown daily since the flooding. As she watches the damage spread, she is pressing the city for answers about the situation near her home.

City public information officer Scott Samples said excess water on the road and in a culvert beneath it caused the damage. Officials are aware of the collapse and are assessing how best to repair it. Samples said the city wants to move quickly, but determining the right approach takes time. “We want to repair these as quickly as we possibly can. Unfortunately, it takes some time,” he said. The city is still working out how to address the damaged area, and Samples said studies may be necessary before crews can begin the repair work. Samples said the city’s goal is to make sure the work is done properly, even if that requires further evaluation before construction starts. “You want to make sure you’re doing it as well and as correctly as you possibly can. So that may require some studies to take place before you actually start the work,” he said. For Duran, the continuing growth of the hole makes answers urgent. “We understand everybody is short-staffed. But we need answers,” she said.

hero.headline: Flood watch canceled for Indian River County; road and school closures remain
hero.body:
The National Weather Service canceled the flood watch for Indian River County Friday morning, while flooding and roadway damage continued to affect travel and the School District of Indian River County remained closed Friday.

Additional showers remain possible, but the heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials urged drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

The county identified these locations among those affected by flooding or roadway damage Friday:

• U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations.
• 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage.
• Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• 130th Street: Closed.
• 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout.
• 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage.
• Vero Lake Estates: 104th Avenue between 87th and 93rd streets, and 83rd Street between 91st and 93rd avenues, are closed.

Drivers can check the county’s live road closure map for additional closures and updates. Officials said water needs time to recede, and damaged roads must be assessed and repaired before they can safely reopen. Crews are working in affected areas, and drivers are asked to give them room and follow barricades.

Marian Fell Library and the Veterans Services office in Sebastian remain closed. The Indian River County Shooting Range, Gifford Aquatic Center and North County Aquatic Center are open Friday. Families can check the School District of Indian River County website for updates on the district closure.

The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

hero.headline: Martin County cancels Kanner Highway data center meeting, promises public forums
hero.body:
Martin County canceled a Friday staff meeting about a proposed data center off Kanner Highway, citing overwhelming public interest, and promised future public meetings and workshops. Residents gathered outside the Martin County Administrative Center anyway, demanding answers about the development west of Interstate 95, roughly half a mile from Crystal Lake Elementary School. The project remains under review and could qualify for administrative approval without a public hearing or a recorded vote by county commissioners.

The county announced the cancellation Thursday evening, less than 17 hours before the meeting was scheduled to begin. Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden said members of the public had requested the informal question-and-answer session with Growth Management Department staff. He said it was intended for questions, rather than a decision on the application, but information circulating online created the impression that officials were privately considering approval. Interest eventually exceeded the county’s capacity to accommodate attendees, he said. “We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size,” Walden said.

The potential approval process is another focus of residents’ objections. A county ordinance adopted in 2010 established administrative approval for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development. Data centers fall within those classifications. Walden said an existing planned unit development agreement also covers the proposal and allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval. Commissioners approved a one-year moratorium on data centers Oct. 27 while the county reviews its development regulations. County officials said this application was submitted before the moratorium was proposed, making the project exempt from that temporary restriction.

Residents raised concerns about potential noise from cooling equipment, water consumption, electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, property values and possible health effects on children at Crystal Lake Elementary School. Those concerns are questions about potential impacts, rather than established consequences of the development. Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from the school, was among those seeking answers Friday. “We need answers, and we need them quick,” he said. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.

Walden said the county will review potential impacts before deciding whether to approve the project. A staff report examining the application is expected in December. After that report, county officials plan a public forum where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development, likely including a presentation from the applicant.

But less than 17 hours before it was scheduled to begin, the county canceled it, citing overwhelming public interest.Residents showed up anyway."We need answers, and we need them quick," said Chris McIntyre, whose son graduated from nearby Crystal Lake Elementary School. "This story cannot die, or else this is the death of Crystal Lake School."McIntyre, who goes by Coach Mack, became emotional discussing what the proposed development could mean for the school and surrounding neighborhoods."Now that's the death of an A-rated elementary school that I love," he said, his voice breaking.He's far from alone.Residents have raised concerns about potential noise pollution, water consumption, increased electricity demand, higher utility bills, wildlife displacement, declining property values and possible health impacts on children attending Crystal Lake Elementary.Michael Panella, another resident opposing the project, became emotional while explaining why the fight is so personal."It's life. These little ones are innocent," Panella said, referring also to students of Crystal Lake. Dan Wilson, president of the Locks Landing homeowners association, represents a community less than two miles from the proposed site.“They’re probably dropping now because, oh, the data center going there. We don’t want to move there,” Wilson said of property values."We have residences right here, tons of residents. We're all going to have to deal with this."Residents acknowledge they don't yet know for sure what the long-term consequences of the project might be. They don't know whether electricity bills will increase, how much noise the facility could generate or what wildlife habitat might be lost.But they do know that once something of this magnitude is built, there's no easy way to undo it.The controversy intensified Thursday evening when Martin County announced the cancellation of an informal Growth Management meeting scheduled for 9:30 a.m. 19, the Martin County Board of County Commissioners posted the following message online:For residents who had planned to attend, the cancellation only added to their frustration."The thing that frustrates me the most about this is the fact that they were willing to do this meeting in private," said resident Alisha Gibbs.Gibbs described herself as "disgusted" and "absolutely appalled" by the situation.But Martin County Deputy Growth Management Director Pete Walden told WPTV Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey that the meeting was never intended to be a formal public hearing or a decision-making session.Instead, Walden said, it was an informal meeting requested by members of the public who wanted to ask county staff questions about the development — something his department routinely accommodates for other projects.He said information about the meeting circulated online, creating the impression that county officials were privately considering a decision on the data center.When interest grew beyond what the county could accommodate, officials decided to cancel."We could not accommodate that. We didn't have any rooms or anything available for that size," Walden explained. "So we had to cancel, and we'll do some workshops in the future. I believe the applicant is also going to reach out for some public presentations on the subject." That timing means the project is not subject to the temporary restriction, according to county officials.Walden acknowledged the timing but said the county cannot control when developers submit applications."They obviously saw like everybody else that a moratorium was coming, and they got their application in ahead of time," Walden said. "We don't direct applicants ... and we certainly can't pick and choose when these things happen."WPTV reached out to the project applicant and the law firm representing it, requesting comment on the timing of the application and residents' environmental, energy and health concerns.Neither responded by publication time.Perhaps the most significant concern for opponents is whether residents will have any formal say in the project's approval.Under a county ordinance adopted in 2010, during the Great Recession, Martin County established an administrative approval process for certain targeted industries to encourage economic development.Data centers fall within the county's targeted industry classifications. According to Walden, the proposed development is also covered by an existing planned unit development, or PUD, agreement that allows qualifying targeted industries on platted industrial lots to receive administrative approval.That means the project could potentially move forward without a public hearing or recorded vote by county commissioners.For residents demanding a voice in the decision, that distinction is critical.Hussey asked Walden whether there was anything the county could do to give residents more of a say in whether the development is approved."With the moratorium, we'll be looking at our code to make revisions so everything is appropriately reviewed as it comes in," Walden said."To give the public more of a say in future projects?" Hussey asked. "Correct," Walden responded. Residents are also demanding answers about how a development of this size could affect surrounding neighborhoods, wildlife and students at Crystal Lake Elementary School.The proposal initially called for just under 1 million square feet of development. An updated application brings the total to approximately 1.6 million square feet, including an existing warehouse.Among the concerns raised by residents are the potential effects of noise from cooling equipment, increased water and electricity consumption, wildlife habitat loss and possible impacts on nearby property values.Those concerns remain questions, not established consequences of the proposed development.Walden said the county will review the project's potential impacts before making any approval decision.He also emphasized that despite speculation circulating in the community, the data center has not been approved."There is a misconception that this project was already approved — that's very far from the truth," Walden said."This is our first data center to be reviewed. We're going to take our time ... and make sure everything is properly vetted."The county says a staff report examining the project is expected to be released in December.Following that report, officials plan to schedule a public forum, likely including a presentation from the applicant, where residents can ask questions and learn more about the development.No date for that meeting has been announced.For opponents, the controversy goes beyond whether a data center belongs on acres of industrial land.It's about who gets to decide what their community becomes — and whether the people who will live with the consequences have a meaningful opportunity to influence that decision.The residents who gathered outside the county building Friday made clear that canceling a meeting would not end their opposition."If they want to actually please the public, they would deny this proposal," Gibbs said.

hero.headline: Flood watch canceled for Indian River County; roads and schools remain closed
hero.body:
The National Weather Service canceled a Flood Watch for Indian River County Friday morning, but flooded and damaged roads remain closed across the county, and the School District of Indian River County is closed Friday.

Additional showers remain possible, though the heaviest rainfall threat is farther north, according to Indian River County Emergency Services. Officials are asking drivers to check road conditions before traveling, allow extra time for detours and never drive through flooded roads.

Flooding or roadway damage was affecting these locations Friday:

• U.S. 1 near Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• Old Dixie Highway SW: Flooding and partial blockages at several locations.
• 82nd Avenue at the entrance to Heritage Plantation: Partial blockage.
• Skyline Drive, from Periwinkle to Barber Street: Partial blockage.
• 130th Street: Closed.
• 79th Street west of 130th Avenue: Closed because of a roadway washout.
• 13th Street SW east of 66th Avenue SW: Closed because of roadway damage.

The county said the list covers selected locations. Drivers can check the county’s live road closure map for additional closures and updates. The county said the Indian River County Fairgrounds may be used in the coming days to support emergency management missions for communities to the north, where the threat of heavy rain and flooding is greater.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie extends boil water notice for about 21,000 customers in Tradition, west areas
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie has extended a precautionary boil water notice affecting about 21,000 customers in Tradition and western neighborhoods after Tuesday's water main break near Glades Cut Off Road. Water quality testing remains underway, and city officials said the notice will stay in place until testing is successfully completed and the city determines it is safe to lift.

The notice covers all of Tradition, including Western Grove, Riverland, Wilson Grove and Southern Grove, as well as areas west of Interstate 95 south to Becker Road. Communities along Glades Cut Off Road, including Copper Creek, Wylder and Verano, are also affected.

City officials said the number of affected customers requires a significant number of water samples to be collected and tested to ensure the water is safe. The city is asking residents not to tamper with clearly marked hydrants or pipes that are flushing water. Interference could delay testing and extend the notice, officials warned.

According to city officials, a contractor working on a construction project unrelated to the city damaged the 36-inch water main. Crews responded and repaired the main within hours, then began the required flushing process.

The city is investigating the incident and expects to pursue appropriate action to recover costs from those responsible. Residents can find updates at CityofPSL.com.

hero.headline: Flooding closes about 12 roads in Indian River County, limits Vero Lake Estates access
hero.body:
About 12 roads were closed in Indian River County Thursday evening as renewed flooding restricted access in Vero Lake Estates. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to avoid unnecessary travel and stay off flooded roads as water continued to affect neighborhoods.

Indian River County Public Schools will be closed Friday because of the flooding. The latest high water comes just weeks after another round of flooding affected parts of the Treasure Coast. County officials reported multiple road closures in Vero Lake Estates, where water surrounding parts of the neighborhood left some residents with limited ways to get around.

Terry Holly, who moved to the area from Pennsylvania with his wife 23 years ago, said his household had supplies to manage the disruption. “We’re stuck another week. Luckily, we’ve got plenty of groceries and water, so we’re all set,” Holly said. He said he and other residents had dropped their flood insurance policies, but repeated flooding has him reconsidering. “We all dropped it. And we haven’t had it since, but now I’m going to rethink it again,” he said.

Holly warned that smaller vehicles could struggle to travel through the standing water. “The trucks and the high vehicles can get through. The small cars, forget it,” he said. Fellow resident Marjorie Hale also raised concerns about traffic, particularly drivers moving too quickly through flooded neighborhoods and the waves their vehicles send toward nearby homes. She said older properties were a particular concern.

Hale said she believes this round of flooding has been handled better than the previous one, with more precautions being taken. Her neighborhood flooded during the earlier round, too. She urged drivers to slow down and consider the people living along flooded streets.

For some families, Friday’s school closure means an early start to Thanksgiving break. Hale said her daughter is old enough to stay home while she works. With other families across the Treasure Coast dealing with more serious flooding and damage to their homes, Hale encouraged neighbors to help one another. “Invite your neighbors to Thanksgiving,” she said.

cards.headline: Vero Beach sets daily rainfall record at 2.25 inches; drier weather expected Sunday
cards.teaser: Thursday’s rainfall topped Vero Beach’s previous daily record of 1.73 inches, set in 1987. A few showers could linger into the weekend before drier weather begins Sunday.
cards.body:
Vero Beach recorded 2.25 inches of rain Thursday, breaking the city’s previous daily rainfall record of 1.73 inches set in 1987. Heavy rain also set a daily record in West Palm Beach, where 3.08 inches fell, surpassing the previous record of 2.99 inches set in 2021. The record-setting totals followed rounds of rain across parts of South Florida and the Treasure Coast. The wet weather has eased, but a few lingering showers remain possible heading into the weekend.

Friday’s forecast calls for cloudy conditions and temperatures near normal for this time of year, with highs in the upper 70s and low 80s. Some areas could have fog during the morning hours. Rain chances remain low, although a stray shower cannot be ruled out.

Saturday is expected to bring a mix of sun and clouds, with temperatures reaching the low 80s. Isolated showers are possible during the afternoon, with rain chances around 30%.

Drier weather is forecast to begin Sunday, and most of next week is expected to stay dry. A cold front approaching Wednesday could bring a few showers. The front is also expected to cool temperatures into the mid-70s by Thanksgiving.

hero.headline: Hobe Sound singer steps in for duet with Matthew Morrison at Maltz Jupiter Theatre
hero.body:
Hobe Sound singer Emily Rynasko joined Broadway and “Glee” star Matthew Morrison for a duet at Maltz Jupiter Theatre after an FAA ground stop prevented much of his ensemble from arriving. Morrison texted Rynasko to ask her to sing with him, giving her only hours to prepare for the performance.

“I found out about 9:30 in the morning, and the show was at 7:30 that night,” Rynasko said. She had watched “Glee” when she was younger and said she never expected an invitation from the actor who played William Schuester. Together, they sang “Somewhere Over the Rainbow.”

Rynasko grew up in Hobe Sound and began her musical training as a child at Maltz Jupiter Theatre. She credited that training, including sight-reading and using her ear, with preparing her to take on the short-notice performance. “It’s being a trained musician that’s part of your job,” Rynasko said. Returning to the theater also meant performing at a place she considers home and among people she considers family.

“I was a lot calmer than I thought I would be because I treated it like any other show that I had done,” Rynasko said. She also spoke about honoring the teachers, community, friends and family who have been part of her journey. “That’s what brings me joy and carries me through.”

hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to close Friday, Nov. 20, amid flooding
hero.body:
All public schools in Indian River County will be closed Friday, Nov. 20, as flooding, waterlogged ground and the chance of additional heavy rain raise safety concerns. The School District of Indian River County announced the closure Thursday, saying it was taking the step to protect students, their families and district employees. The decision comes as roads across parts of the county are closed and water levels are rising at a district transportation facility. The district pointed to a growing number of road closures, especially in Vero Lake Estates, among the conditions behind its decision to keep schools closed Friday.

Flooding also is affecting the district’s North County Transportation compound, where officials reported rising water. Across the county, the road closure map showed nine road closures and four lane closures Thursday. The roads listed as closed included 100th Court, 103rd Avenue, 104th Avenue, 83rd Street and 87th Street. Those five roads were among the closures shown on the map, rather than the full list of affected roads. The Indian River County Sheriff’s Office also reported additional flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates, the same community the school district highlighted when explaining the closure.

The Sheriff’s Office urged drivers to stay out of standing water. Water covering a road can be deeper than it looks, and vehicles can stall if drivers attempt to pass through it. The warning applies to flooded stretches even when a driver cannot easily judge the depth of the water ahead. High-water vehicles are in the area, according to the Sheriff’s Office. Anyone who becomes stranded should call 911. The safety warning comes alongside the reports of more flooded roads in Vero Lake Estates and the road and lane closures listed on the county’s map Thursday.

A flood watch remains in place for Indian River County through Friday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms possible. The National Weather Service reported that parts of eastern Indian River County had received 2 to 4 inches of rain. The possibility of more heavy rain, combined with ground already saturated and localized flooding, was part of the district’s explanation for closing schools. Friday’s closure applies to all of the county’s public schools. Schools also will be closed for Thanksgiving break. For Friday, the district said its decision centers on the safety of students, families and employees amid the flooding and road closures.
